R.q:
Read the description of the pie chart.

Title: How Surveyed Nursing Students Commute to Campus
Total surveyed: 400 students
Sections:
Drive alone: 45%
Public transit: 25%
Carpool: 15%
Walk or bike: 10%
Other: 5%
Note: Students who use more than one method were asked to choose the one they use most often. The survey was emailed to all first- and second-year students in September, and 400 of them completed it.

According to the chart, how many of the surveyed students carpool to campus?
o: 40 students
15 students
100 students
60 students
R.w: The chart shows percentages of 400 students. Carpool is 15%, and 15% of 400 is 0.15 x 400 = 60 students.

n.0: 40 students is the walk-or-bike group (10% of 400).
n.1: Treats the percentage (15%) as a count of students.
n.2: 100 students is the public transit group (25% of 400).

R.q:
Read the passage.

Older adults who volunteer regularly tend to report better health than those who do not. In several long-term studies, retirees who volunteered a few hours a week were less likely to develop high blood pressure and more likely to stay physically active. Researchers think the benefits come partly from staying busy and partly from social contact, since loneliness is linked to poorer health in later life. Volunteering also gives many retirees a sense of purpose that paid work once provided. The studies cannot fully rule out that healthier people are simply more likely to volunteer in the first place. Even with that caution, the pattern has encouraged some senior centers to connect members with local charities.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Loneliness in later life is linked to poorer health among retired adults.
Senior centers should require their members to volunteer with local charities.
Older adults who volunteer tend to be healthier, likely because of activity, contact and purpose.
Researchers cannot yet tell whether volunteering improves health or healthy people volunteer more.
R.w: Most of the passage describes the link between volunteering and better health in older adults and the likely reasons (staying busy, social contact, purpose). The caution about healthier people volunteering is one qualifying sentence, so the main idea keeps the emphasis on the health link.

n.0: Too narrow: the loneliness link is offered as one explanation for the benefits, not as the central point.
n.1: Distortion: senior centers connect members with charities; the passage never says they should require volunteering.
n.3: Reversed emphasis: the caution is a single qualifying sentence, and the author says the pattern holds "even with that caution."

R.q:
A reporter for a local paper is revising a story about a zoning meeting. Her editor has asked her to describe both sides in neutral language so that readers can judge the issue for themselves. Her first draft includes this sentence:

The stubborn residents of Oak Street refused to budge on the cell tower, whining that it would ruin their views.

Which revision presents the residents' position without bias?
o: The residents of Oak Street opposed the cell tower, saying it would block their views.
The residents of Oak Street stubbornly opposed the cell tower, saying it would block their views.
The residents of Oak Street complained repeatedly that the cell tower would block their views.
The determined residents of Oak Street bravely stood against the tower to protect their views.
R.w: "Opposed" and "saying" report the residents' position and reason without judging them. The revision removes "stubborn," "refused to budge" and "whining," which all carried negative connotations.

n.1: "Stubbornly" keeps the negative judgment from the original draft.
n.2: "Complained repeatedly" still frames the residents as whiners, so the negative slant remains.
n.3: "Determined" and "bravely" replace a negative slant with a positive one. Bias in favor of a group is still bias.

R.q:
Dr. Lena Park, the economist who testified in favor of the proposed soda tax, presented data from two cities where soda purchases fell by about 20 percent after similar taxes took effect. But what would she know about the lives of working families? Dr. Park lives in a wealthy suburb, drives a luxury car and has probably never had to stretch a grocery budget. The council should reject this tax.

How does the author mainly attempt to discredit the case for the soda tax?
o: By questioning whether the two cities Dr. Park studied resemble this one
By attacking Dr. Park's personal life instead of responding to her data
By presenting data from other cities that contradict Dr. Park's findings
By explaining how the tax would raise grocery costs for working families
R.w: The author never addresses the 20 percent drop. Instead, the author points to where Dr. Park lives and what she drives. Attacking the person rather than the evidence (an ad hominem attack) is a sign of bias.

n.0: Questioning whether the cities are comparable would be a fair challenge to her evidence, but the author never raises it.
n.2: The author offers no data of any kind; the only figures in the passage are Dr. Park's.
n.3: The author mentions working families but never explains any effect of the tax on grocery costs; the focus stays on Dr. Park herself.

R.q:
Companies should encourage walking meetings for small-group brainstorming. Many offices book every conference room by 9 a.m., and walking meetings need no reserved space. In a university study, participants came up with about 60 percent more creative uses for everyday objects while walking than while sitting. Walking also burns more calories than sitting at a conference table, which may matter to employees who spend most of the day at a desk. "I like getting fresh air in the middle of the day," said one employee at a firm that tried the idea.

Which sentence from the passage best supports the author's main claim?
o: In a university study, participants came up with about 60 percent more creative uses for everyday objects while walking.
"I like getting fresh air in the middle of the day," said one employee at a firm that tried the idea.
Many offices book every conference room by 9 a.m., and walking meetings need no reserved space.
Walking also burns more calories than sitting at a conference table, which may matter to employees who spend most of the day at a desk.
R.w: Step 1: the main claim is about brainstorming, a creative task. Step 2: the study showing about 60 percent more creative ideas while walking supports that specific claim most directly.

n.1: One employee's preference is a weak anecdote and concerns fresh air, not idea generation.
n.2: Room shortages explain a convenience, not why walking meetings improve brainstorming.
n.3: Calories relate to health, a side benefit rather than the brainstorming claim.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a rural clinic director: Since we began offering video visits, patients who once drove ninety minutes for a five-minute medication check can now do it from home. Video works well for follow-ups. Some problems, such as a new lump or chest pain, still require an in-person exam.

Passage 2
From a patient advocate: Telehealth is convenient for many patients, but many older adults in our county lack reliable internet. Insurers should pay for phone-only visits as well as video. Even then, telehealth should add to the clinic, not replace it.

Which statements would both authors most likely agree with? Select all that apply.
o: Follow-up visits work best when they are done by video.
Telehealth makes care more convenient for many patients.
Rural patients are the main users of telehealth services.
Insurers should pay for phone-only visits as well as video.
Most older adults in the county lack internet at home.
Telehealth cannot take the place of every in-person visit.
R.w: The director praises saved drives and the advocate calls telehealth convenient for many. The director says some problems need an in-person exam, and the advocate says telehealth should add to the clinic, not replace it.

n.0: The director says video works well for follow-ups; the advocate does not comment on follow-ups.
n.2: Neither passage compares rural patients with other users.
n.3: Only the advocate calls for phone-only coverage; the director does not address insurance.
n.4: The advocate says many older adults lack reliable internet, not most, and the director does not discuss it.

R.q:
Ethan is researching the 1972 flood that destroyed much of downtown Millbrook. At the county historical society, he finds the following items:
A. A photograph of Main Street taken by a newspaper photographer on the day of the flood
B. An oral history interview, recorded in 2005, with a man who was rescued from his roof in 1972
C. A 2022 newspaper article looking back on the flood's 50th anniversary
D. The Millbrook town council minutes from its emergency meeting in June 1972
E. A local history book, published in 1990, with a chapter analyzing the flood
F. A state encyclopedia entry summarizing major floods in the region

Which items are primary sources? Select all that apply.
o: Item E
Item F
Item C
Item D
Item B
Item A
R.w: The photograph (A) and the council minutes (D) were created during the event. The oral history (B) is an eyewitness account by a survivor, which makes it primary even though it was recorded decades later.

n.0: A history book analyzing the flood interprets primary sources, so it is secondary.
n.1: An encyclopedia entry compiles summaries from other sources, so it is tertiary.
n.2: An anniversary article looks back on and interprets the flood, so it is secondary.

R.q:
Many parents worry that their toddlers are not eating enough vegetables. Children's appetites can change from day to day, and refusing a new food is a normal stage of development. "It can take ten or more tries before a child accepts a new vegetable," says Dr. Maya Thompson, a pediatrician who has studied children's eating habits for fifteen years. Parents can help by serving small portions of new foods next to familiar favorites and by eating the same foods themselves.

Why does the author most likely include the quotation from Dr. Thompson?
o: to support the advice with an expert's credibility
to tell a personal story that appeals to parents' emotions
to introduce a view that the author goes on to argue against
to change the subject from toddlers to older children
R.w: Dr. Thompson's credentials (a pediatrician with fifteen years of research) lend authority to the claim that repeated tries are normal. Using an expert's standing to support a point is an appeal to credibility, or ethos.

n.1: The quotation states a research-based fact rather than a personal story, and its appeal rests on expertise, not emotion.
n.2: The author agrees with Dr. Thompson; the advice that follows builds on her statement.
n.3: The passage stays focused on toddlers; the quotation is about children accepting new vegetables, the same subject.

R.q:
Read the handbook section.

Volunteer Handbook, Section 4: Patient Escort
As you practiced during orientation, lock both wheels of a wheelchair before a patient sits down or stands up. Use the service elevators near the cafeteria rather than the public elevators in the main lobby, which are often crowded during visiting hours. Volunteers do not move patients on stretchers or patients connected to IV pumps; ask the unit clerk to page transport staff instead. If a patient says they feel faint, stop, lock the wheels and call for help using the nearest staff phone.

Which assumption about its readers does the handbook's author most clearly make?
o: Readers have worked as transport staff at other hospitals.
Readers know how to operate IV pumps safely on their own.
Readers have already attended an orientation session.
Readers usually work their shifts during visiting hours.
R.w: The phrase "As you practiced during orientation" shows the author expects readers to have attended orientation already.

n.0: Unsupported: readers are told to ask for transport staff, which suggests they are not transport staff.
n.1: Contradicted: volunteers are told not to move patients connected to IV pumps.
n.3: Unsupported: visiting hours are mentioned only to explain why the lobby elevators are crowded.

R.q:
Read the class schedule.

Community Center Fitness Classes, Fall Session

Water Aerobics | Tue, Thu | 10:00 to 11:00 a.m. | Pool

Zumba

n.1: Water Aerobics meets on weekday mornings, during his work hours.

R.q:
Read the passage.

When Lorraine Whitfield finished nursing school in 1971, the nearest hospital to her hometown in rural Mississippi was a ninety-minute drive away. She spent her first years working night shifts in the city and driving home on weekends to check on neighbors who had no doctor. In 1978 she persuaded a church congregation to donate an old school bus, which she and two volunteers fitted with an exam table, a refrigerator for vaccines and a folding ramp. For the next twenty years, the bus visited eleven towns on a fixed weekly route. By the time Whitfield retired, the county had opened two permanent clinics, both built at stops where the bus had drawn the longest lines.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Lorraine Whitfield worked night shifts in a city hospital before moving back to rural Mississippi.
Rural Mississippi counties needed more hospitals in the 1970s than the state's cities did.
Lorraine Whitfield brought regular care to underserved towns, which helped lead to permanent clinics.
A church donated a school bus that volunteers turned into a mobile clinic in 1978.
R.w: The passage follows Whitfield from seeing the lack of nearby care, to building a mobile clinic, to twenty years of weekly visits, to permanent clinics built at the busiest stops. The main idea links her work to that lasting result.

n.0: Distortion and too narrow: she drove home on weekends, and the passage never says she moved back; this is also only an early detail.
n.1: Too broad and outside the passage: it never compares how many hospitals cities and rural counties needed.
n.3: Too narrow: the donated bus is one event in the story, not the point the whole passage makes.

R.q:
From a district newsletter: Students who used the MathBoost tutoring app for at least 30 minutes a week raised their end-of-semester test scores by an average of 12 points. Students who did not use the app raised their scores by an average of 4 points. MathBoost clearly helps students learn math, and the district should buy licenses for every middle school next year.

Which of the following, if true, would most seriously challenge the claim that the app helps students learn math?
o: Some students in the study used the app for more than two hours each week.
MathBoost would cost the district about $12 per student for each school year.
Most app users were in honors classes that covered more of the tested material.
Students who used the app said they enjoyed its game-style practice lessons.
R.w: Step 1: the claim is that the app caused the larger score gains. Step 2: if most app users were in honors classes that covered more tested material, the class, not the app, could explain the gap.

n.0: Heavy use by some students does not offer another explanation for the score difference.
n.1: Cost bears on whether to buy the app, not on whether it helps students learn.
n.3: Enjoyment is not evidence for or against learning gains.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Telehealth visits grew quickly when many clinics closed their waiting rooms in 2020. Patients who had never used video calls learned to meet their doctors through a phone screen, and many clinics kept offering the option after reopening.

Not every visit works well on a screen, however. A clinician cannot listen to a patient's lungs, feel a swollen joint, or draw blood through a video link. Patients without reliable internet or a private place to talk may struggle to take part. For these reasons, many clinics now use video for follow-up visits and medication checks while asking patients to come in person for new symptoms and physical exams.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the second paragraph?
o: Clinicians cannot examine joints, listen to lungs or draw blood over a video link.
Patients without reliable internet access are unable to take part in telehealth visits.
Telehealth grew rapidly in 2020 and remained common after clinics reopened their doors.
Video visits have limits, so clinics match in-person and video care to the type of visit.
R.w: The second paragraph opens with its topic sentence (not every visit works well on a screen), lists the limits, and ends with the result: clinics use video for some visits and in-person care for others. This option captures both the limits and the response.

n.0: Too narrow: these physical limits are supporting details for the paragraph's point, not the point itself.
n.1: Distortion of one detail: the passage says such patients may struggle, not that they are unable to take part.
n.2: Wrong part of the passage: this is the main idea of the first paragraph, not the second.

R.q:
As a firefighter for 22 years, I have been inside hundreds of homes after a fire, and I have learned which ones families walk out of. Our city should require landlords to install working smoke alarms in every bedroom of every rental unit. Smoke alarms give sleeping families the minutes they need to escape. The cost to a landlord is about $25 per alarm. Tenants should not have to buy their own safety.

In the first sentence, the author mainly uses which type of appeal?
o: Counterclaim, by stating a view the author rejects
Pathos, by describing a frightening fire in detail
Logos, by citing statistics on deaths in rental fires
Ethos, by establishing experience with the topic
R.w: The first sentence tells readers the author has 22 years of firefighting experience inside hundreds of homes. That builds credibility, an appeal to ethos.

n.0: The sentence presents no opposing view; it supports the author's authority.
n.1: The sentence describes the author's experience, not a vivid scene of a particular fire.
n.2: The first sentence gives no statistics; the only figure in the passage is the alarm cost, later.

R.q:
While researching joint supplements for a health class, Marcus finds a polished website called JointHealthFacts. It features charts, quotations from customers, and a list of benefits of a glucosamine product called FlexWell, with a "Buy Now" button on every page. At the bottom of the home page, in small print, a line reads: "This site is owned and operated by FlexWell Nutrition, Inc." The site was updated two months ago.

What is the strongest reason to question this site's credibility?
o: It includes quotations from customers along with its scientific claims.
It is run by the company that profits from sales of the product it praises.
It was last updated two months ago rather than in the past few weeks.
It includes charts and numbers that may be hard for readers to follow.
R.w: The site's purpose is to sell FlexWell, and it is owned by the maker. That conflict of interest is the strongest reason to doubt that its information is balanced.

n.0: Customer quotations are weak evidence, but the deeper problem is who owns the site and why.
n.2: An update two months ago is reasonably current; the date is not the main problem.
n.3: Charts can be hard to read, but using data is not itself a reason to distrust a source.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Dana checked the clock above the nurses' station for the third time in ten minutes. Her coffee had gone cold beside a stack of charts she had not opened. When the elevator chimed, she turned so quickly that her pen rolled off the counter, and when a man with a delivery cart stepped out instead of her daughter's surgeon, she sat back down and pressed her palms flat against the desk. A coworker offered to cover her patients for an hour. Dana shook her head. "I need something to do," she said, and opened the top chart.

Which of the following can the reader infer about Dana?
o: She is expecting a delivery of supplies that she ordered for her unit.
She is irritated that her coworker doubts her ability to work.
She is anxiously waiting for news about her daughter's surgery.
She has fallen behind on her charting because she is new to the unit.
R.w: Several clues combine: she keeps checking the clock, she spins toward the elevator, she slumps when someone other than her daughter's surgeon steps out, and she wants work to keep busy. Together they support anxious waiting for news about the surgery.

n.0: Misreads the scene: she sits back down when the delivery cart appears, showing it is not what she was waiting for.
n.1: Nothing suggests irritation; she declines the offer because she wants something to do, not because she feels doubted.
n.3: The unopened charts reflect distraction; nothing in the passage says she is new or behind for that reason.

R.q:
Passage 1
When I was ten, summer meant leaving the house after breakfast and coming home when the streetlights blinked on. We built forts in the creek bed and settled our arguments ourselves. Those long, unsupervised afternoons taught me how to be a friend.

Passage 2
Every Tuesday night, 12-year-old Amir logs on to a coding club with kids from four states. They debug each other's games, tease each other in the chat, and celebrate birthdays on video. Two of them met in person for the first time this summer and hugged like old friends.

How do the themes of the two passages differ?
o: Passage 1 is about friendship, while Passage 2 is about learning to write code.
Both passages suggest that children today are lonelier than children once were.
Passage 1 rejects technology, while Passage 2 rejects outdoor play for children.
Passage 1 ties friendship to outdoor play; Passage 2 shows it growing through screens.
R.w: Both passages are about how children form friendships. Passage 1 credits unsupervised outdoor play; Passage 2 shows close friendships forming in an online coding club.

n.0: Coding is the setting of Passage 2, but its central idea is friendship, the same subject as Passage 1.
n.1: Passage 2 shows children who are close and connected, so loneliness is not a shared theme.
n.2: This overstates both: Passage 1 never criticizes technology, and Passage 2 never criticizes outdoor play.

R.q:
Passage 1
After thirty years with the fire department, Walt retired and found the days long and quiet. On a friend's advice, he began training puppies to become service dogs. Now he spends his mornings teaching them to open doors and pick up dropped keys, and he says he has not felt this useful since his last shift.

Passage 2
When her husband died, Joan stopped going out except to walk her terrier. A neighbor invited her to a community choir, and she went once, then every week. Two years later, Joan organizes the choir's concerts at local hospitals and calls Tuesday rehearsal "the best night of my week."

Which theme do both passages share?
o: A new commitment can restore purpose after a major change.
Music helps people work through grief after a death.
Retirement is harder for people who did physical work.
Pets give steady comfort to people who live on their own.
R.w: Walt finds purpose in training service dogs after retiring, and Joan finds it in the choir after her husband's death. Both show a new commitment filling the gap left by a major life change.

n.1: This fits Passage 2 only; Passage 1 involves no music or death.
n.2: This draws on Passage 1 only and goes beyond it; Passage 1 does not compare kinds of work.
n.3: Dogs appear in both, but that is a minor shared detail; Joan's change comes from the choir, not her terrier.

R.q:
Read the email.

From: Priya Raman, Lab Coordinator
To: Nursing Cohort 2026
Subject: Change to Thursday's skills check-off
Sent: Tuesday, 3:14 p.m.

Hi everyone,
Because the simulation lab's air conditioning is being repaired, Thursday's IV skills check-off is moving from Lab 2 to Room 118 in the Allied Health building. The time is unchanged (1:00 to 4:00 p.m.), but please arrive 15 minutes before your assigned slot instead of 10. Bring your own gloves; the kits in Room 118 do not include them. If your slot is after 3:00, you may leave your bag in the student lounge next door.
Thanks, Priya

Darnell's assigned slot on Thursday is 2:30 p.m. According to the email, where and when should he arrive?
o: Room 118 at 2:15 p.m.
The student lounge at 2:15 p.m.
Room 118 at 2:20 p.m.
Lab 2 at 2:15 p.m.
R.w: The check-off has moved to Room 118, and students must now arrive 15 minutes before their slot: 2:30 minus 15 minutes is 2:15 p.m.

n.1: The lounge is for leaving bags, and only for students with slots after 3:00.
n.2: Uses the old 10-minute arrival rule, which the email replaces with 15 minutes.
n.3: Lab 2 is the old location; the check-off has moved to Room 118.

R.q:
(1) Every year, the Ridgeview public pool opens on Memorial Day and closes on Labor Day. (2) Yet the hottest weeks in our town now often arrive in September, when the pool sits empty behind a locked gate. (3) Ridgeview should keep the pool open through the end of September. (4) Last year, the high temperature topped 90 °F on eleven September days. (5) Some council members worry about the cost of lifeguards once college students return to school. (6) But the high school swim team has offered certified lifeguards on weekends, and extra admission fees would cover weekday staff.

Which sentence states the author's main claim?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
Sentence 6
R.w: Sentence 3 states the position the whole letter defends: keep the pool open through September. The other sentences give reasons, evidence, an objection, and a response to it.

n.1: Sentence 2 is a reason for the claim (the hot weeks have shifted), not the position itself.
n.2: Sentence 4 is evidence, a statistic supporting the reason in Sentence 2.
n.3: Sentence 6 is a rebuttal that answers the cost objection raised in Sentence 5.

R.q:
Before her baby is born, Hannah wants to choose a rear-facing car seat that performs well in crashes. She has found the websites of three car seat makers, a federal safety agency's page that compares the results of crash tests it ran on many seats, an online store's list of best-selling car seats, and a video by a popular parenting influencer who was paid by one brand to review its seat.

Which source is most reliable for comparing crash safety?
o: The car seat makers' websites, because they know their own products best
The influencer's video, which shows the seat being installed and used
The federal safety agency's page, which compares results of its crash tests
The online store's list of best sellers, which shows what parents choose
R.w: An independent government agency that runs the same crash tests on many seats provides authoritative, comparable data with no product to sell.

n.0: Each maker has a financial interest in promoting its own seat, and their claims are not directly comparable.
n.1: The influencer was paid by the brand, which is a conflict of interest, and a video demonstration is not crash testing.
n.3: Sales rankings show popularity, not crash performance.

R.q:
Opponents of the city's plan to put calorie counts on restaurant menus argue that diners do not read them and that the signs will only raise costs for small businesses. It is true that calorie labels alone will not solve obesity. But a 2018 study of a large restaurant chain found that customers ordered about 4 percent fewer calories after labels appeared, and many restaurants quietly made their dishes lighter. Those small changes add up across millions of meals. The council should pass the measure.

With which statement would the author most likely agree?
o: Calorie labels offer small benefits that add up over time.
Most diners do not read calorie counts printed on menus.
Calorie labels are not worth the cost to small businesses.
Calorie labels by themselves can solve the problem of obesity.
R.w: The author argues that a 4 percent reduction and lighter recipes "add up across millions of meals" and urges the council to pass the measure. Small but meaningful benefits sum up the author's view.

n.1: This is the opponents' claim, which the author reports in order to rebut it. A view the author reports is not necessarily the author's own.
n.2: This is also the opponents' argument; the author supports the measure despite the cost concern.
n.3: The author concedes that labels "alone will not solve obesity," so the author would reject this claim.

R.q:
Burns are grouped into types according to how deeply they damage the skin. A superficial burn, often called first-degree, affects only the outer layer of skin and causes redness and pain. A partial-thickness burn, or second-degree burn, reaches into the layer below and usually forms blisters. A full-thickness burn, or third-degree burn, destroys both layers and may look white, brown or leathery. Because nerve endings can be destroyed, a full-thickness burn may cause less pain than a smaller, shallower one.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: classification
chronological order
spatial order
cause and effect
R.w: The opening sentence says burns are "grouped into types," and the rest of the passage defines each type by its depth. Sorting a subject into categories is classification.

n.1: The types are listed by depth, not in time order; no events unfold.
n.2: Skin layers are mentioned, but the passage is not a description of where things are located in space; it defines categories.
n.3: The last sentence explains one cause and effect (destroyed nerves, less pain), but that detail sits inside the larger classification.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

A clerk starts with this list of five patient names: Ortiz, Baker, Nguyen, Patel, Fischer. She carries out the steps below in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Arrange the names in alphabetical order.
2. Move the name in the third position to the end of the list.
3. Swap the first and second names.
4. Move Patel to the front of the list.

Place the names in the order they appear after step 4, starting with the first.
o: Baker
Fischer
Ortiz
Nguyen
Patel
R.w: Step 1: Baker, Fischer, Nguyen, Ortiz, Patel. Step 2 moves Nguyen (third) to the end: Baker, Fischer, Ortiz, Patel, Nguyen. Step 3: Fischer, Baker, Ortiz, Patel, Nguyen. Step 4: Patel, Fischer, Baker, Ortiz, Nguyen.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Returning Your Sample Kit
Seal the sample tube inside the clear biohazard bag, but first wrap the tube in the absorbent pad. Place the sealed bag in the white box. After the bag is in the box, slip the completed request form into the box's outer pocket; do not put the form inside the bag. Once the form is in the pocket, tape the box shut, and drop it off at any post office within 24 hours of collecting the sample.

Place the steps in the order the directions require, starting with the first.
o: Slip the request form into the outer pocket
Place the sealed bag in the white box
Drop the box off at a post office
Seal the tube inside the biohazard bag
Wrap the tube in the absorbent pad
Tape the box shut
R.w: The first sentence is written out of order: "but first" means the tube is wrapped in the pad before it is sealed in the bag. The sealed bag then goes in the box, the form goes in the outer pocket after the bag is in the box, the box is taped once the form is in place, and it is dropped off.

R.q:
Because the medication can harm a developing fetus, it is contraindicated during pregnancy. For this reason, pharmacists ask every patient of childbearing age whether she might be pregnant before filling the prescription, and the label carries a bold warning on the front of the bottle.

As used in the passage, the word contraindicated most nearly means
o: prescribed at a lower dose than usual.
required by the prescriber.
less effective during pregnancy.
advised against because of risk.
R.w: "Because" links the harm to a fetus with the word, and the pharmacist's screening and bold warning show the drug should not be used in pregnancy. Contraindicated means advised against because it may cause harm.

n.0: A lower dose would still mean using the drug; the warnings and screening point to avoiding it.
n.1: This is close to the opposite; the context describes steps taken to keep pregnant patients from receiving the drug.
n.2: The concern in the passage is harm to the fetus, not whether the drug works less well.

R.q:
After her first two evening shifts at the new urgent care center, Brianna told her roommate, "Both nights, the waiting room was nearly empty by 9 p.m. People in this town obviously don't use urgent care in the evening. The center should close at 8 and save money on staff." The center had opened the week before, during a holiday, when many families were out of town.

Which fallacy does Brianna's reasoning contain?
o: Appeal to tradition
Post hoc
Circular reasoning
Hasty generalization
R.w: Brianna draws a broad conclusion about the whole town's habits from two nights, and those nights fell during an unusual holiday week. That is a hasty generalization from too few, unrepresentative examples.

n.0: She makes no appeal to how things have always been done; the center is brand new.
n.1: Brianna does not claim that one event caused a later one; she generalizes from a small sample.
n.2: Her conclusion rests on observations, not on a restatement of itself; the problem is the tiny sample.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The storm reached Port Allen just after midnight. While the wind tore shingles from roofs along the harbor, volunteers at the high school had already been setting up cots in the gym for two hours; they had begun at ten o'clock, right after the mayor ordered the evacuation of the low-lying east side. The power failed at 1:30 a.m., and the hospital switched to its backup generators within seconds. At dawn, the first rescue boats went out to the east side, where floodwater had reached the second step of many porches. By noon the water had begun to drop.

According to the passage, which event happened immediately before volunteers began setting up cots?
o: The power failed and the hospital started its generators.
The storm reached Port Allen just after midnight.
The wind tore shingles from roofs along the harbor.
The mayor ordered the evacuation of the east side.
R.w: Volunteers began at ten o'clock, "right after the mayor ordered the evacuation." The storm, the wind damage and the power failure all came later, after midnight.

n.0: The power failed at 1:30 a.m., long after the volunteers began at ten.
n.1: Order of mention trap: the storm is mentioned first but arrived after midnight, two hours after the cots were started.
n.2: The wind damage happened while the volunteers were already working, after midnight.

R.q:
The Okafor family is planning a day hike in the mountains tomorrow and wants to know whether thunderstorms are expected on the trail in the afternoon. They have found a National Weather Service seasonal outlook calling for a wetter-than-normal summer, the National Weather Service forecast for the hiking area that was updated this morning, this morning's forecast for their home city two hours' drive away, and a park ranger's post from yesterday about muddy conditions on the trail.

Which source should the family use?
o: The park ranger's post from yesterday about muddy conditions on the trail
This morning's forecast for their home city, two hours' drive from the trail
The National Weather Service forecast for the hiking area, updated this morning
The National Weather Service seasonal outlook calling for a wetter summer
R.w: The hiking-area forecast meets every need: it is current (updated this morning), covers the exact place and day, and comes from the national weather authority.

n.0: The ranger's post concerns the trail but describes yesterday's ground conditions, not a forecast of tomorrow's storms.
n.1: This forecast is current but covers a city two hours away; it does not describe afternoon storms in the mountains where they will hike.
n.3: The outlook comes from the right agency, but it covers the whole season, not tomorrow afternoon in the hiking area.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Before a new vaccine reaches a pharmacy shelf, it passes through several stages. The large phase 3 trial, which can include tens of thousands of volunteers, comes after a smaller phase 2 trial has helped researchers choose the right dose. Phase 2, in turn, follows phase 1, in which a few dozen healthy adults receive the vaccine so that researchers can check its safety. None of these human trials can begin until laboratory and animal studies suggest the vaccine is promising. If phase 3 shows that the vaccine is safe and effective, the company applies to the Food and Drug Administration for a license. Even after licensing, safety monitoring continues.

Place the stages in the order in which they occur, starting with the first.
o: Continued safety monitoring after licensing
Phase 2 trial to help choose the dose
Phase 1 trial in a few dozen healthy adults
Laboratory and animal studies
Phase 3 trial with thousands of volunteers
Application to the FDA for a license
R.w: The passage describes the stages backward. Laboratory and animal studies come before any human trial; phase 1 comes before phase 2, which comes before phase 3; a license is sought after phase 3; monitoring continues after licensing.

R.q:
Several nurses on 4 West have proposed moving the morning shift change from 7:00 to 6:30 a.m. so that handoff reports finish before the 7:00 medications are due. They point out that nurses now give morning medications late on most days. The unit manager rejected the idea: "Shift change has been at 7:00 since this hospital opened in 1974. It has worked for fifty years, and I see no reason to change it now."

Which fallacy does the manager's response contain?
o: Hasty generalization
False dilemma
Bandwagon
Appeal to tradition
R.w: The manager defends the 7:00 shift change because it has been done that way since 1974, without answering the nurses' point about late medications. Arguing that something is right because it is long-standing is an appeal to tradition.

n.0: The manager does not generalize from a few examples.
n.1: The manager does not reduce the issue to two options.
n.2: Bandwagon appeals to what many people currently do or believe; the manager appeals to history.

R.q:
The company claims its new wristband can detect dehydration before the wearer feels thirsty. Perhaps it can. But the company has not released any test data, and the two reviewers who wore the device during the same workout got readings that differed by 30 percent. Until an independent lab checks these claims, I would hold off on spending $199 for one. I'll believe it when I see the numbers.

Which word best describes the author's tone?
o: hostile
cynical
pessimistic
skeptical
R.w: The author doubts the claim but stays open to evidence ("Perhaps it can," "I'll believe it when I see the numbers"). Doubt that waits for proof is a skeptical tone.

n.0: "Hostile" suggests anger or attack; the author's language is measured and practical.
n.1: A cynical writer distrusts people's motives and assumes the worst. This author does not accuse the company of lying and allows that the device might work.
n.2: "Pessimistic" means expecting a bad outcome. The author withholds judgment until data arrive instead of predicting failure.

R.q:
Our county should require bicycle helmets for riders under 16. Head injuries are the leading cause of serious harm in bicycle crashes, and a helmet that fits correctly greatly lowers the risk of a brain injury. In the past three years, the county trauma center treated 46 children for head injuries from bike crashes, and only 5 of them had been wearing helmets. Helmets now cost as little as $15, and the fire department gives them away free at every spring safety fair. A helmet rule would protect our children at little cost to families.

Which element of a complete argument is missing from the passage?
o: A clear claim that the author wants readers to accept
A reason explaining why the claim deserves support
A response to an objection that opponents might raise
Evidence that supports the reasons behind the claim
R.w: The passage states a claim, gives reasons (head injuries, low cost), and supports them with evidence (46 children, 5 in helmets; $15 helmets). It never raises or answers an opposing view, such as concerns about enforcement or personal choice.

n.0: The first sentence states the claim directly: require helmets for riders under 16.
n.1: The passage gives reasons: helmets lower brain injury risk and cost families little.
n.3: The trauma center figures and the helmet prices are evidence.

R.q:
Keisha is writing a history paper on how the 1918 influenza pandemic affected her hometown of Clearwater. The county historical society lets her view its collection, and the reference librarian at the public library suggests several more items. She wants at least one source that comes directly from someone who lived through the outbreak in Clearwater, so she can quote that person's own observations.

Which source should Keisha use for this purpose?
o: A documentary film in which historians discuss the pandemic's effects
A 2010 book by a historian about the pandemic in small American towns
An encyclopedia entry that summarizes the 1918 influenza pandemic
A letter written in October 1918 by a Clearwater nurse to her sister
R.w: A letter written by a Clearwater nurse during the outbreak is a primary source: a firsthand account created at the time by someone who witnessed the events.

n.0: A documentary built on historians' commentary analyzes events after the fact, so it is secondary.
n.1: A historian's book written about 90 years later interprets earlier sources, so it is secondary.
n.2: An encyclopedia compiles and summarizes information from other sources, so it is tertiary.

R.q:
The safety committee's report was succinct. In just two pages, it summarized six months of meetings, listed three recommendations and set a deadline for each. Board members, who were used to reports of fifty pages or more, praised the committee for its clarity and approved all three recommendations at the same meeting.

As used in the passage, the word succinct most nearly means
o: brief and to the point.
carefully and thoroughly researched.
easy to understand.
strongly worded.
R.w: "In just two pages" and the contrast with reports of "fifty pages or more" point to length. Succinct means brief and to the point.

n.1: Six months of meetings shows effort, but the clues next to succinct describe how short the report was, not how it was researched.
n.2: This matches a nearby word, "clarity," which describes a separate quality the board praised. The clues tied to succinct are about length.
n.3: Nothing describes the tone of the recommendations; the passage focuses on the report's length.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium. The skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to sunlight, but people who live far from the equator make much less of it in winter, when the sun stays low in the sky. A survey in one northern state found that more residents had low vitamin D levels in February than in August. Few foods contain much vitamin D naturally; fatty fish and egg yolks are two exceptions. Many brands of milk and breakfast cereal have vitamin D added during processing.

Based on the passage, which statement is supported?
o: People in northern states should take vitamin D supplements throughout the winter.
Low vitamin D was more common in the surveyed state in late winter than in late summer.
Milk is one of the best natural sources of vitamin D for most people in the country.
A lack of vitamin D causes the bones of adults to soften and weaken over time.
R.w: The passage reports that more residents of the northern state had low levels in February (late winter) than in August (late summer), which matches the explanation about weaker winter sunlight.

n.0: A recommendation the passage never makes.
n.2: Distortion: the passage says vitamin D is added to milk, so milk is not a natural source.
n.3: Outside knowledge: the passage says vitamin D helps absorb calcium but says nothing about bones softening.

R.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The human body has two kinds of sweat glands. Eccrine glands, found over most of the skin, release a watery sweat that cools the body as it evaporates. They are especially dense on the palms, the soles of the feet and the forehead.

(2) Apocrine glands are found mainly in the armpits and groin. They become active at puberty and release a thicker fluid containing proteins and fats. This fluid has no odor of its own; body odor develops when bacteria on the skin break it down.

(3) Both types are controlled by the nervous system, but they respond to different signals. Most eccrine glands respond mainly to heat, while apocrine glands respond mainly to emotional stress, which is why a nervous person may notice damp armpits even in a cool room.

According to paragraph 2, what causes body odor?
o: Watery eccrine sweat evaporating from the palms, soles and forehead
Emotional stress, which signals the apocrine glands to release their fluid
Proteins and fats in apocrine fluid, which have a strong odor of their own
Bacteria on the skin breaking down the fluid released by apocrine glands
R.w: Paragraph 2 states that apocrine fluid has no odor of its own and that body odor develops when bacteria on the skin break it down.

n.0: Wrong part of the passage: paragraph 1 describes eccrine sweat, which cools the body.
n.1: Wrong part of the passage: paragraph 3 says stress triggers apocrine glands to release fluid, which explains sweating, not odor.
n.2: Contradicts paragraph 2, which says the fluid has no odor of its own.

R.q:
Supporters of the proposed ban on plastic grocery bags claim it will cut litter in our parks in half. The evidence from cities that have tried such bans suggests a smaller effect: studies in three comparable cities found that plastic bag litter fell, but overall park litter dropped by about 20 percent. Even so, I will vote for the ban. A 20 percent drop is real progress, the cost to shoppers is a reusable bag, and our parks crew spends hundreds of hours a year picking up plastic.

Which statement best expresses the author's own position?
o: The ban is worth adopting even if its effect is smaller than claimed.
The ban will cut park litter in half, as its supporters have claimed.
The ban should be rejected because its effect on park litter is modest.
The city should study the ban for another year before it votes on it.
R.w: The author doubts the supporters' 50 percent claim, citing a drop of about 20 percent, but says "Even so, I will vote for the ban" because that drop is real progress.

n.1: This is the supporters' claim, which the author reports and then questions.
n.2: The author calls the effect modest but supports the ban anyway.
n.3: The author does not call for more study and states a plan to vote for the ban.

R.q:
The school board is considering two plans. Plan A, proposed by a group of parents and pediatricians, would move the high school start time from 7:20 to 8:30 a.m. Its supporters cite research showing that teenagers who start school later sleep more, miss fewer days and are involved in fewer car crashes. They note that districts in several states have made the change with strong results. Plan B, from the transportation office, would keep the current schedule to save on bus costs.

The author's bias is most evident in the way the passage
o: explains that the second plan would keep the current schedule to reduce bus costs.
states the exact current and proposed start times for the high school day.
supports one plan with detailed evidence but gives the other one sentence.
identifies the parents, pediatricians and transportation staff who proposed each plan.
R.w: Plan A gets research findings, several benefits and examples from other districts, while Plan B gets one sentence and no evidence. Unequal treatment of the two sides is a sign of bias, even when no single word is openly loaded.

n.0: Stating Plan B's purpose is fair to that side; the bias lies in how little support Plan B receives compared with Plan A.
n.1: The start times are neutral, checkable details.
n.3: Naming who proposed each plan is balanced; both sources are identified.

R.q:
Passage 1
At mile 22 of her first marathon, Gloria's left calf cramped so badly that she sat down on the curb. Volunteers offered her a ride to the finish. She shook her head, stood, and walked, then jogged, one streetlight at a time. She crossed the line after the clocks had been switched off.

Passage 2
When the river flooded the Ashton library, it ruined 30,000 books. For eight months, volunteers sorted donations on folding tables in the high school gym, a few boxes each evening. Last week, the library reopened with full shelves and a new reading room.

Which theme do both passages share?
o: Finishing a hard race matters more than the time on the clock.
Steady effort, step by step, can carry people through great difficulty.
Floods and other disasters test the resources of small towns.
Communities grow stronger when neighbors give their time to one another.
R.w: Gloria finishes by going one streetlight at a time, and the library is rebuilt a few boxes each evening over eight months. Both show persistence in small steps overcoming a setback.

n.0: This fits Passage 1 only; Passage 2 is not about a race.
n.2: This names a topic of Passage 2 and does not apply to Passage 1.
n.3: Community volunteering fits Passage 2, but Gloria turns down help and finishes on her own.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Five books stand on a shelf. From left to right they are Atlas, Biology, Chemistry, Dictionary and Encyclopedia. A library aide carries out the steps below in order, applying each step to the arrangement left by the step before it.
1. Move Dictionary to the far left.
2. Swap the books in the second and fifth positions.
3. Move the book that is now in the middle one place to the right.
4. Reverse the order of the first three books only.

Place the books in their final order from left to right, starting with the leftmost.
o: Dictionary
Atlas
Biology
Chemistry
Encyclopedia
R.w: Step 1: Dictionary, Atlas, Biology, Chemistry, Encyclopedia. Step 2 swaps Atlas and Encyclopedia: Dictionary, Encyclopedia, Biology, Chemistry, Atlas. Step 3 moves Biology (middle) one place right: Dictionary, Encyclopedia, Chemistry, Biology, Atlas. Step 4 reverses the first three: Chemistry, Encyclopedia, Dictionary, Biology, Atlas.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Bayview Community College: Associate Degree in Nursing
Program Length: The program takes four semesters to complete after prerequisites. Most students finish in two years, attending full time.
Clinical Experience: Students complete 180 hours of supervised clinical practice in the first year and 240 hours in the second year, for a total of 420 hours. First-year clinicals take place at Bayview General Hospital; second-year students may also rotate through the county health department and two long-term care centers.
Skills Lab: In addition, each semester includes 45 hours in the on-campus simulation lab, where students practice procedures on mannequins before performing them with patients.

According to the passage, how many hours of supervised clinical practice does a student complete in the second year?
o: 240 hours
420 hours
330 hours
180 hours
R.w: The Clinical Experience section states 240 hours of supervised clinical practice in the second year.

n.1: 420 hours is the total for both years.
n.2: Adds the second year's two semesters of simulation lab (90 hours), which the passage lists separately from clinical practice.
n.3: 180 hours is the first-year figure.

R.q:
You wake at 4:30 a.m., before the alarm, because your body has learned the schedule. You pull on scrubs in the dark so you will not wake anyone, grab the lunch you packed last night and drive through empty streets to the hospital. By 6:45 you are taking report from the night nurse, and by 7:15 you have already answered three call lights. Your feet ache by noon. Still, when a patient squeezes your hand and thanks you, you remember why you chose this work.

From which point of view is the passage written?
o: first person
third person limited
third person objective
second person
R.w: The narration addresses the reader directly as "you" and places the reader in the role of the nurse. That is second-person point of view.

n.0: The passage reads like a personal memory, but no "I" or "we" appears; every action is assigned to "you."
n.1: Third-person limited would describe a character as "he" or "she" and reveal that character's thoughts.
n.2: Third-person objective would describe characters from outside using "he" or "she," reporting only actions and speech.

R.q:
Read the description of the line graph.

Title: Average Wait Time at Two Urgent Care Centers, by Time of Day
Legend: solid line = North Center; dashed line = South Center
Vertical axis: Average wait (minutes)
Plotted values (solid, dashed):
8 a.m.: 15, 25
10 a.m.: 20, 30
12 p.m.: 35, 30
2 p.m.: 40, 20
4 p.m.: 30, 15
6 p.m.: 25, 35
Values are averages for weekday visits during March.

A patient can visit either center at either 2 p.m. or 4 p.m. Based on the graph, which choice gives the shortest expected wait?
o: South Center at 4 p.m.
North Center at 4 p.m.
North Center at 2 p.m.
South Center at 2 p.m.
R.w: South Center is the dashed line. Its values are 20 minutes at 2 p.m. and 15 minutes at 4 p.m. North Center (solid) shows 40 and 30. The shortest of the four is South Center at 4 p.m., 15 minutes.

n.1: Swaps the legend: 15 minutes at 4 p.m. belongs to the dashed line (South); North's wait at 4 p.m. is 30 minutes.
n.2: North Center at 2 p.m. shows the longest wait of the four choices, 40 minutes.
n.3: South Center at 2 p.m. is 20 minutes, 5 minutes longer than at 4 p.m.

R.q:
Using Your Metered-Dose Inhaler

1. Remove the cap and shake the inhaler well for five seconds.
2. Breathe out fully, away from the inhaler.
3. Place the mouthpiece between your teeth and close your lips around it.
4. Press down on the canister once while breathing in slowly and deeply.
5. Hold your breath for 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly.
6. If a second puff is prescribed, wait one minute, shake the inhaler again and repeat steps 2 through 5.
7. If your inhaler contains a steroid, rinse your mouth with water after each use.

Which feature of this text most clearly marks it as technical writing rather than expository writing?
o: It numbers each action the reader must take, in order.
It uses a title that names the subject of the text.
It leaves out opinions and emotional language.
It presents accurate information about a medical device.
R.w: Technical (procedural) texts give exact, ordered directions for doing a task or using equipment. The numbered commands ("Remove," "Breathe out," "Hold your breath") set this text apart from an expository text, which explains a topic without walking the reader through actions step by step.

n.1: Expository articles also have titles naming their subject, so a title does not identify a text as technical.
n.2: Expository writing is also neutral and free of opinion, so this feature is shared by both types rather than distinguishing them.
n.3: Expository texts also present accurate information, so accuracy does not separate the two types.

M.q: A survey at a health fair found that 7 of every 20 visitors had their blood pressure checked. If 1,260 people visited the fair, how many would be expected to have had their blood pressure checked?
M.w: Set up 7/20 = x/1,260. Cross-multiply: 20x = 8,820, so x = 441.

n.0: This divides 1,260 by 7 instead of multiplying by 7/20.
n.1: This is 1/20 of the visitors, the size of one part, not 7 parts.
n.2: This is the number expected not to have had a check (13 of every 20).

M.q: A closed cylindrical can has a radius of 3 inches and a height of 8 inches. A paper label covers the curved side of the can but not the top or bottom. What is the area of the label? Use 3.14 for pi.
M.w: Unrolled, the label is a rectangle: circumference × height. Area = 2πrh = 2 × 3.14 × 3 × 8 = 150.72 in².

n.0: This uses πrh; the curved side's area is 2πrh (circumference × height).
n.1: 226.08 is the volume (πr²h) in cubic inches, not the label's area.
n.2: This adds the top and bottom circles (2 × 28.26 in²); the label covers the curved side.

M.q: The mean of 8 blood glucose readings is 115 mg/dL. When one reading is removed, the mean of the remaining 7 readings is 110 mg/dL. What was the value of the removed reading, in mg/dL?

tr.120: 115 + 5, adding the change in the mean
tr.112.5: the average of the two means

M.w: Total of 8 readings = 8 x 115 = 920. Total of 7 readings = 7 x 110 = 770. Removed reading = 920 - 770 = 150 mg/dL.

M.q: A dietitian estimates a man's resting calorie needs with the expression 10w + 6.25h - 5a + 5, where w is weight in kilograms, h is height in centimeters, and a is age in years. What value does the expression give for w = 80, h = 175, and a = 40?

n.1: This leaves off the constant + 5 at the end of the expression.
n.2: This adds 5a instead of subtracting it: the expression has - 5a, so 200 is taken away.
n.3: This treats the final + 5 as - 5, which makes the result 10 lower.

M.q: A traveler rents a car in Canada, where gasoline costs $1.70 per liter. The car's tank holds 12 gallons. Use 1 gallon = 3.785 liters. How much will it cost to fill the empty tank? Enter the number of dollars, rounded to the nearest dollar.

tr.5: Divided 12 by 3.785 (3.17 L) instead of multiplying.
tr.20: Multiplied 12 by $1.70 without converting gallons to liters.

M.q: Three coworkers split a $47.83 lunch bill equally. Each person's share is rounded up to the next cent so that the bill is fully covered. How much does each person pay?
M.w: $47.83 ÷ 3 = $15.9433... Rounding up to the next cent gives $15.95. Check: 3 × $15.95 = $47.85, which covers the bill.

n.0: $16.00 rounds up to the next dollar, not the next cent.
n.2: $15.90 rounds down to the nearest ten cents and leaves the bill short.
n.3: $15.94 is ordinary rounding; 3 × $15.94 = $47.82, which is 1 cent short.

M.q: A research lab recorded five room temperatures, some in degrees Celsius and some in degrees Fahrenheit. Place the readings in order from coldest to warmest, starting with the coldest.
M.w: Convert the Celsius readings to °F with °F = (9/5)(°C) + 32: 14 °C = 57.2 °F; 15 °C = 59 °F; 16.5 °C = 61.7 °F. Coldest to warmest: 57.2 °F (14 °C), 58 °F, 59 °F (15 °C), 61 °F, 61.7 °F (16.5 °C).

M.q: A clinic buys 38 boxes of syringes at $19.75 per box. Rounding each number to the nearest ten, which is the estimate of the total cost?
M.w: 38 rounds to 40 and $19.75 rounds to $20. Estimate: 40 × $20 = $800. (The exact cost is $750.50.)

n.0: $400 rounds $19.75 down to $10; the ones digit 9 means rounding up to $20.
n.1: $300 truncates both numbers (30 × $10) instead of rounding.
n.2: $600 rounds 38 down to 30; the ones digit 8 means rounding up to 40.

M.q: A clinic's trend line for monthly advertising spending, x (in hundreds of dollars), and new patients, y, is y = 4x + 30. In March the clinic spent $1,200 on advertising and gained 70 new patients. How does March compare with the trend line's prediction?
o: 35.2 more than predicted
8 more than predicted
8 fewer than predicted
22 more than predicted
M.w: $1,200 is 12 hundred dollars, so x = 12. Predicted y = 4(12) + 30 = 78. Actual 70 is 78 - 70 = 8 fewer than predicted.

n.0: Using x = 1.2 (thousands) gives 4.8 + 30 = 34.8; x is in hundreds, so x = 12.
n.1: The size is right, but 70 is below 78, so March was under the prediction.
n.3: 70 - 48 = 22 uses 4 x 12 and leaves out the 30 in the equation.

M.q: A rectangular park is 240 meters long and 100 meters wide. Instead of walking along two sides of the park to reach the opposite corner, a jogger takes a straight diagonal path. How many meters shorter is the diagonal route? Enter the number of meters.

tr.200: Used 240 - 100 = 140 m as the diagonal instead of the Pythagorean theorem.
tr.260: Gave the length of the diagonal instead of the distance saved.
tr.340: Gave the distance along the two sides instead of the distance saved.

M.q: A 24-ounce bag of brown rice costs $4.56. A 2.5-pound bag of the same rice costs $7.20. Which bag costs less per ounce, and by how much?
o: The 24-oz bag, by $0.01 per ounce
The 2.5-lb bag, by $0.01 per ounce
The 24-oz bag, by $2.64 per package
The 24-oz bag, by $0.10 per ounce
M.w: 24-oz bag: $4.56 ÷ 24 = $0.19 per ounce. 2.5-lb bag: 2.5 × 16 = 40 oz, and $7.20 ÷ 40 = $0.18 per ounce. The 2.5-lb bag is cheaper by $0.19 - $0.18 = $0.01 per ounce.

n.0: This reverses the comparison; $0.18 per ounce is less than $0.19 per ounce.
n.2: $2.64 compares the bag prices, not the price per ounce.
n.3: $0.10 per ounce uses 1 lb = 10 oz (25 oz in the bag); 1 lb = 16 oz.

M.q: A taxi company sets the cost of a ride, C, based on the number of miles driven, m. Which statement correctly identifies the variables in this relationship?
o: C is independent, because it is the amount the rider pays
m is independent, and C depends on m
m is dependent, because it is measured during the ride
Both are dependent, because each changes with the other
M.w: The cost is calculated from the miles, so miles (m) is the input, or independent variable, and cost (C) is the output, or dependent variable.

n.0: The amount paid is the result of the miles driven, which makes C dependent.
n.2: Being measured does not make a variable dependent; m is the input that sets the cost.
n.3: One variable is the input and the other the output; C changes because m changes, not the reverse.

M.q: Marcus's phone plan costs $35 per month plus $0.10 for each text message over 200. His bill for March was $47.40. How many text messages did he send in March?
M.w: Let t = texts over 200: 35 + 0.10t = 47.40, so 0.10t = 12.40 and t = 124. Total texts sent = 200 + 124 = 324.

n.1: This subtracts the extra texts from 200 instead of adding them to 200.
n.2: This is the number of texts over the 200 included texts. The total sent is 200 + 124 = 324.
n.3: This divides the whole $47.40 bill by $0.10 without first removing the $35 monthly charge.

M.q: An audit of patient charts on a unit found that 5/6 of the charts were fully complete. Which percentage is equivalent to 5/6?
M.w: 5 ÷ 6 = 0.8333..., a repeating decimal. As a percent this is 83.333...% = 83 1/3%. Check: 1/6 = 16 2/3%, and 5 × 16 2/3% = 83 1/3%.

n.1: 120% = 6/5. This divides the denominator by the numerator.
n.2: 8 1/3% = 0.08333..., which moves the decimal point in 0.8333... only 1 place right.
n.3: 62 1/2% is the benchmark for 5/8, not 5/6.

M.q: What is the value of (-3) × 4 × (-2) × (-1) ÷ (-6)?
M.w: Multiply left to right: (-3)(4) = -12; (-12)(-2) = 24; (24)(-1) = -24. Then -24 ÷ (-6) = 4. There are four negative signs (an even number), so the result is positive.

n.0: -4 miscounts the negative signs; there are four negatives, an even number, so the result is positive.
n.1: 144 multiplies -24 by -6 instead of dividing.
n.2: -144 multiplies by -6 instead of dividing and also miscounts the signs.

M.q: A large set of adult cholesterol levels is roughly symmetric and bell-shaped, with a mean of 190 mg/dL and a standard deviation of 20 mg/dL. Which statement is best supported?
o: About 68% of the levels fall between 170 and 210 mg/dL
About 95% of the levels fall between 170 and 210 mg/dL
About half of the levels are above 210 mg/dL
About 68% of the levels fall between 150 and 230 mg/dL
M.w: In a bell-shaped distribution, about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean: 190 - 20 = 170 to 190 + 20 = 210.

n.1: 170 to 210 is within 1 standard deviation, which holds about 68%, not 95%.
n.2: About half are above the mean of 190; only about 16% are above 210.
n.3: 150 to 230 is within 2 standard deviations, which holds about 95%, not 68%.

M.q: On a floor plan, 1 inch represents 4 feet. A rectangular room on the plan measures 3 inches by 2.5 inches. What is the actual area of the room?
o: 7.5 ft²
30 ft²
44 ft²
120 ft²
M.w: Actual sides: 3 × 4 = 12 ft and 2.5 × 4 = 10 ft. Area = 12 × 10 = 120 ft². (Check: 7.5 in² × 16 = 120 ft².)

n.0: 7.5 is the area on the plan in square inches, not the actual area.
n.1: This multiplies the plan's area (7.5 in²) by 4; areas scale by 4 × 4 = 16.
n.2: 44 ft is the actual perimeter (2 × 12 + 2 × 10), not the area.

M.q: A researcher graphs how the dose of a pain reliever, in milligrams, affects the time until a patient reports relief, in minutes. How should the axes of the graph be labeled?
o: Dose on the y-axis, because the dose is what the researcher controls
Time until relief on the x-axis, because time is the independent variable
Either variable on either axis, since the graph shows a correlation
Dose on the x-axis and time until relief on the y-axis
M.w: The independent variable (dose, which the researcher sets) goes on the x-axis, and the dependent variable (time until relief, which responds) goes on the y-axis.

n.0: The variable the researcher controls is independent and belongs on the x-axis, not the y-axis.
n.1: Time is often independent, but here the time until relief is the response to the dose, so it is dependent.
n.2: Convention places the independent variable on the x-axis so the graph shows how y responds to x.

M.q: A patient's fluid intake on Tuesday was 7/4 of the daily target set by the care team. Which percentage of the target did the patient take in?
M.w: 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75. Multiply by 100 to write it as a percent: 1.75 × 100 = 175%. A value greater than 1 is more than 100%.

n.0: 1.75% puts a percent sign on 1.75 without multiplying by 100.
n.1: 17.5% = 0.175. The decimal point in 1.75 was moved only 1 place right.
n.2: 57.1% is 4 ÷ 7, the reciprocal of 7/4.

M.q: A data set of daily exercise minutes for seven patients is 4, 6, 7, 7, 9, 10, 41. If the value 41 is removed from the data set, how do the mean and the median change?
o: The mean falls by about 4.8; the median falls to 6.5
The mean and median both fall by about 4.8
The mean falls by about 4.8; the median stays at 7
The mean falls by about 5.9; the median stays at 7
M.w: Before: mean = 84 / 7 = 12, median = 7. After: 4, 6, 7, 7, 9, 10 has mean 43 / 6 = 7.17 and median (7 + 7) / 2 = 7. The mean drops by about 4.8; the median does not change.

n.0: 6.5 averages 6 and 7, but the two middle values of the six remaining are 7 and 7.
n.1: The median is resistant to the outlier: the two middle values are both 7, so it stays at 7.
n.3: 41 / 7 = 5.9 is the outlier's share of the old mean, but the new mean is computed over 6 values: 12 - 7.17 = 4.8.

M.q: A news graph titled 'ER Visits Explode' shows yearly visits at one hospital. The vertical axis runs from 4,000 to 4,600, and the years 2019, 2021, and 2024 are spaced equally along the horizontal axis. Which features make the graph misleading? Select all that apply.
o: The vertical axis begins at 4,000 instead of 0
The title states a conclusion the data may not support
The years are evenly spaced despite unequal gaps
The vertical axis is labeled with the number of visits
A line is used to show change over time
M.w: A truncated vertical axis exaggerates changes, equal spacing for unequal gaps (2 years, then 3 years) distorts the rate of change, and a loaded title pushes a conclusion before the reader checks the scale.

n.3: Labeling the axis with what is counted is good practice and helps readers.
n.4: A line graph is the appropriate display for change over time.

M.q: A number line runs from 0 to 2, with tick marks every 1/4 unit starting at 0. Point A is on the 7th tick mark to the right of 0. What is the value of point A?
M.w: Each tick is 1/4 unit, so 7 ticks to the right of 0 is 7 × 1/4 = 7/4 = 1 3/4.

n.0: 7/8 treats each tick as 1/8, as if the 8 intervals covered 0 to 1 instead of 0 to 2.
n.1: 1 1/2 = 6/4 counts the tick at 0 as the first tick mark.
n.3: 1.7 treats each tick as 0.1; the ticks are quarters, not tenths.

M.q: A community health fair needs at least $1,500 in donations. So far it has raised $612. Each sponsor table brings in $85. What is the least number of additional sponsor tables needed to reach the goal? Enter a whole number.

tr.10: Rounded 10.45 down; 10 tables leave the fair $38 short.
tr.18: Divided the whole $1,500 by $85 without subtracting the $612 already raised.

M.w: Write 612 + 85t ≥ 1,500. Subtract 612: 85t ≥ 888. Divide by 85: t ≥ 10.45. Tables are whole, so round up to 11. Check: 10 tables raise $850 (total $1,462, short); 11 raise $935 (total $1,547).

M.q: A clinic scheduled 80 appointments on Tuesday, and 12 patients did not show up. What percent of the scheduled appointments were kept?
M.w: Appointments kept: 80 - 12 = 68. Percent kept = 68 ÷ 80 × 100 = 85%.

n.0: This subtracts 12 ÷ 68 from 100%. The whole is the 80 scheduled appointments.
n.1: This is the no-show rate, 12 ÷ 80, not the percent of appointments kept.
n.2: This divides 12 by 68, using the kept appointments as the whole instead of all 80 scheduled.

M.q: A 1,000 mL IV bag starts infusing at 0800 at 125 mL per hour. At 1130 the rate is reduced to 75 mL per hour. Assuming the infusion continues without stopping, how many milliliters remain in the bag at 1400? Enter the number of milliliters only.

tr.250: Used 125 mL per hour for all 6 hours.
tr.550: Used 75 mL per hour for all 6 hours.
tr.625: Gave the volume infused instead of the volume remaining.

M.q: A cylindrical water tank behind a rural clinic has a radius of 3 feet and a height of 5 feet. What is the volume of the tank? Use 3.14 for pi.
o: 94.2 ft³
47.1 ft³

n.1: This uses the diameter (6 ft) as the radius.
n.2: This uses 2πrh, the area of the curved side, instead of πr²h.
n.3: This multiplies pi by the radius once (3.14 × 3 × 5) instead of by r².

M.q: A pie chart shows the blood types of 400 patients. Of these patients, 152 have type O blood. What is the central angle of the type O sector?
M.w: Fraction of the whole: 152 / 400 = 0.38. Central angle = 0.38 x 360° = 136.8°.

n.1: 38 is the percent (38%), not the angle; it must be multiplied by 360° as a decimal.
n.2: 152 is the number of patients, not degrees.
n.3: 0.62 x 360° = 223.2° is the angle for all the patients who are not type O.

M.q: A medical assistant counts 23 heartbeats in 20 seconds. At this rate, what is the patient's heart rate in beats per minute? Enter the number of beats per minute.

tr.46: Doubled the 20-second count instead of tripling it.
tr.1.15: Divided 23 by 20 to get beats per second and stopped.

M.w: One minute is 60 seconds, which is 3 × 20 seconds. Heart rate = 23 × 3 = 69 beats per minute.

M.q: A punch recipe mixes 3 cups of juice with 5 cups of sparkling water. How many cups of juice are needed to make 14 cups of punch? Enter the number of cups.

tr.8.4: Used the part-to-part ratio 3/5 as the fraction of the punch that is juice.
tr.8.75: Found the amount of sparkling water instead of juice.

M.w: The recipe makes 3 + 5 = 8 cups, and 3 of those 8 cups are juice. Juice = 3/8 × 14 = 5.25 cups.

M.q: A quality report lists four measurement errors: -9.2, 9.15, 8.7 and -8.95. Which error has the greatest absolute value?
M.w: Absolute value is distance from 0: |-9.2| = 9.2, |9.15| = 9.15, |8.7| = 8.7, |-8.95| = 8.95. The greatest is 9.2, from -9.2.

n.0: 9.15 is the greatest number, but its distance from 0 (9.15) is less than 9.2.
n.2: |-8.95| = 8.95, which is less than 9.2.
n.3: |8.7| = 8.7, the smallest absolute value of the four.

M.q: Of the 640 students in a prerequisite course, 45% are taking the TEAS this semester, and 75% of those students plan to apply to a BSN program. How many students in the course plan to apply?
M.w: Taking the TEAS: 0.45 × 640 = 288. Planning to apply: 0.75 × 288 = 216. (Equivalently, 0.45 × 0.75 = 0.3375 and 0.3375 × 640 = 216.)

n.1: This takes 75% of all 640 students instead of 75% of the 288 taking the TEAS.
n.2: This subtracts the percents (75% - 45% = 30%) and takes 30% of 640. A percent of a percent is found by multiplying.
n.3: This is the number taking the TEAS; 75% of those 288 students still has to be found.

M.q: A 12-pack of bottled water costs $5.40, and a 30-pack of the same bottles costs $12.90. How much less per bottle does the 30-pack cost than the 12-pack?

n.0: $0.43 is the price per bottle in the 30-pack, not the difference.
n.1: $0.20 places the decimal point one place too far right in the difference.
n.3: $7.50 is the difference between the package prices, not the per-bottle prices.

M.q: In a data set of 20 hospital stays, the longest stay, 9 days, is entered by mistake as 90 days. Which statistic stays the same despite the error?
o: The range
The standard deviation
The median
The mean
M.w: The median depends on the middle values (the 10th and 11th of 20). Changing the largest value does not move the middle, so the median is unchanged.

n.0: The maximum changes from 9 to 90, so the range grows by 81.
n.1: The new extreme value lies far from the mean, which increases the spread.
n.3: The total rises by 81, so the mean rises by 81 / 20 = 4.05 days.

M.q: Jasmine spent 1/4 of her paycheck on rent and 1/3 of her paycheck on groceries. She had $350 left. What was the amount of her paycheck?

n.0: This treats $350 as 1/3 of the paycheck. The amount left is 5/12 of the paycheck.
n.2: This adds the fractions as 1/4 + 1/3 = 2/7, leaving 5/7. The correct sum is 3/12 + 4/12 = 7/12.
n.3: This divides $350 by 7/12, the fraction she spent. The $350 is the fraction left over, 5/12.

M.q: A wound measured 3.4 centimeters long when it was assessed on Monday. On Friday, the same wound measured 27 millimeters long. By how many millimeters did the length of the wound decrease?
o: 7 mm
0.7 mm
313 mm
M.w: 3.4 cm × 10 = 34 mm. Decrease = 34 - 27 = 7 mm.

n.1: This subtracts 3.4 from 27 without first converting 3.4 cm to millimeters.
n.2: 0.7 is the decrease in centimeters; 0.7 cm = 7 mm.
n.3: This converts 3.4 cm to 340 mm by multiplying by 100; 1 cm = 10 mm.

M.q: A home health agency charges C dollars for a visit lasting h hours, where C = 45h + 30. In this equation, what does the 30 represent?
o: The number of hours covered by the base fee
The total cost of a 1-hour visit
The cost for each hour of the visit
A flat $30 fee on top of the hourly charge
M.w: In C = 45h + 30, the constant 30 is the y-intercept: the cost when h = 0. It is a fixed fee added to the $45 per hour.

n.0: 30 is in dollars, not hours, and the equation includes no free hours.
n.1: A 1-hour visit costs 45(1) + 30 = $75.
n.2: The cost per hour is the slope, 45.

M.q: Pharmacy A fills 135 prescriptions in 9 hours. Pharmacy B fills 48 prescriptions in 2 hours 40 minutes. How many more prescriptions per hour does Pharmacy B fill than Pharmacy A?
M.w: Pharmacy A: 135 ÷ 9 = 15 per hour. Pharmacy B: 2 hours 40 minutes = 2 2/3 hours = 160 minutes; 48 ÷ 160 = 0.3 per minute × 60 = 18 per hour. Difference: 18 - 15 = 3.

n.1: This reads 2 hours 40 minutes as 2.4 hours, giving 48 ÷ 2.4 = 20 per hour for Pharmacy B.
n.2: This is Pharmacy B's rate, not the difference between the two rates.
n.3: This is Pharmacy A's rate, not the difference between the two rates.

M.q: An advertisement compares a clinic's flu vaccination rate in 2020 and 2025. The rate doubled, so the artist drew the 2025 syringe picture twice as tall and twice as wide as the 2020 picture. Why is the graphic misleading?
o: The 2025 picture is twice as wide, so it understates the increase
The 2025 picture has 2 times the area, which shows the doubling accurately
The 2025 picture has 8 times the area, suggesting an eightfold increase
The 2025 picture has 4 times the area, so the increase looks larger than double
M.w: Scaling both dimensions by 2 multiplies the area by 2 x 2 = 4. Readers judge pictures by area, so a doubling looks like a fourfold increase.

n.0: The extra width makes the increase look larger, not smaller.
n.1: Doubling the height and the width multiplies the area by 4, not 2.
n.2: A factor of 8 (2 x 2 x 2) applies to volume; a flat picture scales its area by 4.

S.q: A woman who is a carrier of hemophilia A (XHXh) and a man without hemophilia (XHY) plan a family. What percentage of their sons are expected to have hemophilia? Enter a whole-number percent.

tr.0: assumed a son inherits X-linked alleles from the father
tr.25: gave the share of all children affected, not of sons
tr.100: assumed every son of a carrier is affected

S.w: Sons get the Y from the father and one X from the mother. Half of the mother's eggs carry Xh, so 1/2 = 50% of sons (XhY) are expected to have hemophilia.

S.q: A nursing student moves from a coastal city to a mountain town about 2,500 m above sea level. What should she predict about the boiling point of water when she cooks pasta there?
o: Higher, because the air pressure is higher
Higher, because the air pressure is lower
Lower, because the air pressure is lower
Lower, because the air pressure is higher
S.w: Air pressure falls as altitude rises (an inverse relationship). Water boils when its vapor pressure matches the air pressure, so lower air pressure means water boils at a lower temperature.

n.0: Air pressure is lower, not higher, at altitude, and higher pressure would raise the boiling point.
n.1: Lower air pressure lowers the boiling point; the direction of the effect is reversed.
n.3: The boiling point is lower, but because air pressure decreases with altitude, not increases.

S.q: Tyler wonders why the houseplants near his window lean toward the glass. Place the steps of the scientific method in the order he should follow them, starting with the first.
o: Conduct an experiment
Draw a conclusion
Ask a question
Analyze the data
Make an observation
Form a hypothesis
S.w: The scientific method runs: observation (plants lean toward the window), question (why?), hypothesis (a testable prediction), experiment (test it), data analysis, then a conclusion that supports or rejects the hypothesis. Results are then communicated, and the cycle repeats if the hypothesis is rejected.

S.q: A student grows bean plants with 0, 5, 10 or 15 g of fertilizer per pot, using the same soil, pot size and daily water. After three weeks she measures each plant's height. What is the dependent variable?
o: Plant height after three weeks
Type of soil used in each pot
Mass of fertilizer in each pot
Volume of water given each day
S.w: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to the change; here, plant height. The fertilizer mass is what she deliberately changes (independent variable).

n.1: Soil type is kept the same in every pot, so it is a controlled variable.
n.2: Fertilizer mass is the independent variable: the factor the student deliberately changes.
n.3: Daily water is held constant, so it is a controlled variable.

S.q: A student is sorting pairs of variables for a study guide on relationships. Which pairs show an inverse relationship? Select all that apply.
o: Altitude and the boiling point of water
Gas volume and kelvin temperature at constant pressure
Altitude and air pressure
Generations of binary fission and bacterial count
Gas pressure and volume at constant temperature
Enzyme activity and temperature below the optimum
S.w: In an inverse relationship, one variable rises as the other falls: gas pressure rises as volume falls; air pressure falls as altitude rises; and the boiling point falls as altitude rises.

n.1: Gas volume rises with kelvin temperature at constant pressure, a direct relationship.
