n.3: Bacterial count rises with each generation (exponential growth), so both increase together.
n.5: Below the optimum, enzyme activity rises with temperature, a direct relationship.

S.q: A student is reviewing the three subatomic particles before a quiz. Which statements about these particles are correct? Select all that apply.
o: The mass number equals protons plus electrons
The number of protons equals the atomic number
Electrons are found in the nucleus with the protons
Protons and neutrons have about the same mass
Electrons have about the same mass as protons
Neutrons carry no electrical charge
S.w: Protons and neutrons each have a mass of about 1 amu, neutrons are neutral (charge 0), and the atomic number is defined as the number of protons.

n.0: Mass number counts the particles in the nucleus: protons plus neutrons, not electrons.
n.2: Electrons occupy energy levels in the electron cloud around the nucleus; only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.
n.4: An electron's mass is about 1/1836 of a proton's, which is why electrons are ignored in the mass number.

S.q: A science club is choosing a question for its next investigation. Which claim can be investigated scientifically?
o: Schools should require students to sleep 8 hours a night.
Dreams carry hidden messages that no measurement can detect.
Students ought to value sleep more than late-night study.
Students who sleep 8 hours score higher on memory tests.
S.w: Scientific claims must be testable and falsifiable with empirical evidence. Sleep hours and memory scores can both be measured and compared.

n.0: This is a policy recommendation about what ought to happen; data can inform it, but no observation can test an 'ought'.
n.1: A claim defined as undetectable by any measurement cannot be falsified, so it cannot be investigated scientifically.
n.2: This is a value judgment about what students should care about, which cannot be measured objectively.

S.q: A student's carefully controlled experiment produces data that do not support her hypothesis. According to the scientific method, what is the most appropriate response?
o: Report the results and revise the hypothesis for further testing
Reword the hypothesis to fit the data and report it as confirmed
Discard the results because the experiment did not work
Repeat the same trial until one result supports the hypothesis
S.w: Results that fail to support a hypothesis are still valid findings. The scientist reports them, revises the hypothesis and tests again; science is iterative.

n.1: A hypothesis rewritten after seeing the data has not been tested by those data, so it cannot be called confirmed.
n.2: A controlled experiment that rejects a hypothesis has worked; negative results are informative.
n.3: Repeating until a favorable result appears is cherry-picking, which biases the conclusion.

S.q: Glucose enters a muscle cell through GLUT carrier proteins, moving from a higher concentration in the blood to a lower concentration in the cell. No ATP is used. Which process is this?
o: Pinocytosis by vesicles
Active transport by a pump
Facilitated diffusion
Simple diffusion across the bilayer
S.w: Movement down a concentration gradient through a carrier or channel protein, without ATP, is facilitated diffusion.

n.0: Pinocytosis takes in droplets of fluid by vesicle and uses ATP; it is not carrier-mediated transport of single molecules.
n.1: Active transport uses ATP and moves substances from low to high concentration. A carrier protein alone does not make transport active.
n.3: Simple diffusion passes straight through the bilayer with no protein. Glucose is too large and polar to do that.

S.q: Place the structures in the order oxygenated blood passes through them after leaving the lungs, starting with the first.
o: Mitral valve
Aorta
Left atrium
Pulmonary vein
Left ventricle
Aortic valve
S.w: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle, and is pumped through the aortic valve into the aorta and the systemic circulation.

S.q: When a skeletal muscle fiber is stimulated, calcium ions flood the sarcoplasm. To which protein do these calcium ions bind directly to begin the process of contraction?
o: Tropomyosin
Troponin
Actin
Myosin
S.w: Ca²⁺ binds troponin on the thin filament. This shifts tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads can form cross-bridges.

n.0: Tropomyosin is the strand that covers actin's binding sites; it is moved by troponin, not bound by Ca²⁺.
n.2: Actin carries the binding sites for myosin; calcium acts on troponin, which then uncovers those sites.
n.3: Myosin heads bind actin and ATP; calcium does not bind myosin to start skeletal muscle contraction.

S.q: A new digital thermometer is compared with a reference reading of 37.0 °C. Its four readings are 36.4, 37.6, 36.9 and 37.1 °C, which average 37.0 °C. Which description fits these results?
o: Accurate on average but not precise
Both precise and accurate overall
Shifted high by a systematic error
Precise but off from the reference
S.w: The mean equals the reference value, so the readings are accurate on average. They spread over 1.2 °C, so they are not precise, like darts scattered around the bullseye.

n.1: Readings that differ by up to 1.2 °C from one another are not precise.
n.2: A systematic error shifts readings one way; these fall on both sides of 37.0 °C and average to it.
n.3: The readings spread over 1.2 °C, so they are not precise, and their mean matches the reference.

S.q: A lab analysis shows that an unknown macromolecule from a cell contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, but no phosphorus. Which type of macromolecule is it most likely to be?
o: A nucleic acid
A protein
A carbohydrate
A phospholipid
S.w: Step 1: nitrogen rules out carbohydrates and simple fats. Step 2: the absence of phosphorus rules out nucleic acids and phospholipids, leaving protein (C, H, O, N, often S).

n.0: Nucleic acids contain phosphorus in their phosphate groups.
n.2: Common carbohydrates such as sugars, starch and glycogen contain only C, H and O, so nitrogen points away from them.
n.3: Phospholipids contain a phosphate group, so phosphorus would be present.

S.q: A student builds a model of one DNA nucleotide for a biology display. Which three components should the model include?
o: An amino group, a carboxyl group and an R group
A phosphate group, a ribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, deoxyribose and a nitrogenous base
Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group
S.w: A nucleotide is a phosphate group + a 5-carbon sugar + a nitrogenous base. In DNA the sugar is deoxyribose.

n.0: An amino group, carboxyl group and R group are the parts of an amino acid, the monomer of proteins.
n.1: Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides; DNA uses deoxyribose.
n.3: Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate make up a phospholipid, not a nucleotide.

S.q: A student is reviewing a data table and must flag every value that contains exactly three significant figures. Which values should be flagged? Select all that apply.
S.w: 0.00250 has 3 (leading zeros do not count; the trailing zero after the decimal does). 2.50 has 3 (trailing zero after a decimal point counts). 205 has 3 (a zero between nonzero digits counts).

n.0: 0.025 has 2 significant figures; the leading zeros are placeholders.
n.2: 0.002500 g has 4 significant figures: the 2, the 5 and both trailing zeros after the decimal point.
n.4: With no decimal point, the trailing zero in 250 is not counted as significant, giving 2 significant figures.

S.q: Carbon dioxide entering the blood at the tissues is rapidly combined with water to form carbonic acid, which then releases bicarbonate. Where does the enzyme that speeds this reaction act?
o: Carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells
Carbonic anhydrase dissolved in the plasma
Surfactant lining the alveolar walls
Hemoglobin inside the red blood cells
S.w: Carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells catalyzes CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃. Carbonic acid releases H⁺ and HCO₃⁻, and most of the bicarbonate then moves out into the plasma for transport.

n.1: The bicarbonate ends up mostly in plasma, but the enzyme that makes it works inside red blood cells.
n.2: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and is not an enzyme for CO₂ conversion.
n.3: Hemoglobin carries O₂ and some CO₂ and buffers H⁺, but it is not the enzyme that forms carbonic acid.

S.q: Tapping the patellar tendon makes the leg kick forward, while stepping on a tack makes the foot pull away. How does the patellar reflex differ from this withdrawal reflex?
o: It depends on conscious awareness in the cerebral cortex
It has no interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons
It uses an interneuron, while the withdrawal reflex does not
It is processed in the cerebellum before the motor response
S.w: The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is monosynaptic: the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron in the spinal cord. Withdrawal reflexes use interneurons.

n.0: Reflexes are rapid and involuntary; the spinal cord processes them before the brain is aware.
n.2: This reverses the two: withdrawal reflexes use interneurons, and the patellar reflex does not.
n.3: Both reflexes are processed in the spinal cord; the cerebellum is not part of the reflex arc.

S.q: Researchers isolate a new bacterium from every sick animal in an outbreak and grow it in pure culture. According to Koch's postulates, what should they do next?
o: Treat the sick animals with an antibiotic and record recovery.
Re-isolate the bacterium from a newly infected animal.
Find the bacterium in each diseased animal in the outbreak.
Introduce the cultured bacterium into a healthy animal.
S.w: Koch's postulates: (1) the microbe is found in all diseased hosts, (2) it is isolated and grown in pure culture, (3) it causes the disease when introduced into a healthy host, (4) it is re-isolated from that host. Steps 1 and 2 are done, so step 3 is next.

n.0: Treating with antibiotics is not one of Koch's postulates and would not show that the microbe causes the disease.
n.1: Re-isolating the microbe is the final step (4); it can only follow infection of a healthy host.
n.2: Finding the microbe in all diseased hosts is step 1, which the researchers have already done.

S.q: Shortly after a meal high in fat, cells of the duodenum release a hormone that makes the gallbladder contract. Which hormone is this, and what other effect does it have?
o: Secretin; it also triggers pancreatic bicarbonate release
Glucagon; it also triggers glycogen breakdown
Gastrin; it also triggers gastric acid secretion
Cholecystokinin; it also triggers pancreatic enzyme release
S.w: Cholecystokinin (CCK) from the duodenum makes the gallbladder contract to release bile and stimulates the pancreas to release its digestive enzymes.

n.0: Secretin does trigger bicarbonate release from the pancreas, but it is not the hormone that contracts the gallbladder.
n.1: Glucagon is a pancreatic islet hormone that raises blood glucose; it is not a duodenal hormone.
n.2: Gastrin comes from the stomach and stimulates acid secretion; it does not contract the gallbladder.

S.q: A student mixes two clear, colorless solutions in a test tube. Within seconds, a cloudy yellow solid forms and slowly settles to the bottom. What does this observation most likely indicate?
o: A chemical change, because a precipitate has formed
A physical change, because two liquids were mixed
A physical change, because the solid can be filtered off
A chemical change, because the mixture is now uneven
S.w: The formation of a precipitate (an insoluble solid) from two solutions is a sign of a chemical change: a new substance with new properties has been produced. Other signs include unexpected gas, color change, light and temperature change.

n.1: Mixing alone can be physical, but here a new solid substance appeared, which signals a reaction.
n.2: Being able to separate the solid by filtration does not make the change physical; the solid is a newly formed substance.
n.3: The change is chemical, but the reason is the new substance; a heterogeneous mixture can also form by purely physical mixing.

S.q: A pharmacist prepares an iodine tincture by dissolving a small amount of solid iodine in a much larger volume of ethanol, with no water added. Which choice correctly identifies the parts of this solution?
o: Iodine is the solute; ethanol is the solvent
Ethanol is the solute; iodine is the solvent
Both are solutes, because no water is present to dissolve them
Iodine is the solute; the tincture is the solvent
S.w: The solute is the substance being dissolved (usually the smaller amount), and the solvent is the substance doing the dissolving (usually the larger amount). Water is the most common solvent, but in a tincture the solvent is alcohol: iodine is the solute and ethanol is the solvent.

n.1: This reverses the roles: the iodine is the substance being dissolved, and the ethanol, present in the larger amount, does the dissolving.
n.2: Water is the most common solvent, but not a requirement; here ethanol, the larger amount, does the dissolving, so it is the solvent.
n.3: The tincture is the whole solution, not one of its parts; the solvent is the ethanol that dissolves the iodine.

S.q: A reversible reaction in a sealed container is allowed to run until it reaches dynamic equilibrium. Which statement is true once equilibrium is reached?
o: Forward and reverse rates are equal; amounts hold steady
Reactant and product concentrations have become equal
The forward rate is faster, so products keep building up
Both reactions have stopped, so the amounts stay constant
S.w: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant, though usually not equal to each other.

n.1: Concentrations become constant, not necessarily equal; an equilibrium mixture can be mostly products or mostly reactants.
n.2: If the forward rate were faster, the system would not yet be at equilibrium.
n.3: Amounts are constant, but both reactions keep running; equilibrium is dynamic, not stopped.

S.q: A patient stops taking a prescribed antibiotic after three days because she feels better. Why can this practice contribute to antibiotic resistance?
o: The drug makes each bacterium change to resist it.
Her body itself becomes resistant to the antibiotic.
Viruses in her body learn to resist antibiotics.
Surviving bacteria tend to be the most resistant ones.
S.w: An incomplete course kills the most susceptible bacteria first; the survivors are more likely to carry resistance, and they multiply. This is natural selection, and resistance genes can also spread on plasmids.

n.0: Antibiotics do not make bacteria change on purpose; they select bacteria that already carry resistance.
n.1: Resistance is a property of the bacteria, not of the patient's body.
n.2: Antibiotics do not act on viruses, so viral resistance to them is not the issue.

S.q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is described as a strong acid, while the acetic acid in vinegar is a weak acid. What does the term 'strong' refer to?
o: How completely the acid ionizes in water
How many hydrogen atoms each molecule holds
How concentrated the acid solution is
How much base is needed to neutralize it
S.w: Acid strength refers to the degree of ionization: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely in water, while a weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partially.

n.1: The number of hydrogen atoms does not set strength; acetic acid (CH₃COOH) has four hydrogens but is weak.
n.2: Concentration is how much acid is dissolved in a volume; a strong acid can be dilute and a weak acid concentrated.
n.3: The amount of base needed depends on the moles of acid present, not on whether the acid is strong or weak.

S.q: When blood pressure suddenly rises, stretch receptors in large arteries signal the brain, which then slows the heart rate. Which statement correctly identifies the type of feedback and the heart's role?
o: Positive feedback; the heart acts as the effector
Negative feedback; the heart acts as the receptor
Negative feedback; the heart acts as the effector
Positive feedback; the heart acts as the control center
S.w: Two steps. Slowing the heart reverses the rise in pressure, so this is negative feedback (the baroreceptor reflex). The heart carries out the response directed by the brain, so it is the effector.

n.0: The heart is the effector, but the response opposes the rise in blood pressure, which is negative feedback.
n.1: This is negative feedback, but the receptors are the stretch receptors in the arteries; the heart produces the response.
n.3: The response opposes the change (negative feedback), and the control center is the brain, not the heart.

S.q: During a 10-second sprint, a runner quickly uses up the ATP already stored in the leg muscles. Which source then regenerates ATP most rapidly for the next several seconds?
o: Oxygen stored on myoglobin
Aerobic respiration in mitochondria
Creatine phosphate
Anaerobic glycolysis
S.w: Muscle energy sources come into play in sequence: stored ATP (a few seconds), then creatine phosphate, which transfers its phosphate to ADP almost instantly (about 10 to 15 seconds), then anaerobic glycolysis, then aerobic respiration.

n.0: Myoglobin stores oxygen for aerobic respiration; it does not regenerate ATP directly.
n.1: Aerobic respiration yields the most ATP but is the slowest pathway, so it is not the most rapid source.
n.3: Anaerobic glycolysis is fast but follows creatine phosphate as the main source after the first several seconds.

S.q: Early versions of the periodic table placed the elements in order of increasing atomic mass. In the modern periodic table, the elements are arranged in order of increasing which quantity?
o: Number of valence electrons
Atomic mass
Number of neutrons
Number of protons
S.w: The modern table (after Moseley) is arranged by increasing atomic number, which is the number of protons. Mendeleev's earlier table used atomic mass.

n.0: Valence electrons repeat in each period (1 through 8), so they set the group, not the overall order.
n.1: Atomic mass was Mendeleev's ordering; a few pairs (such as tellurium and iodine) are out of mass order in the modern table.
n.2: Neutron number varies between isotopes and does not increase steadily across the table.

S.q: Glucose reacts completely with oxygen in a combustion-type reaction: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → ? Which products correctly complete the balanced equation?
o: 6 CH₂O + 6 O₂
6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O
6 CO + 6 H₂O + 3 O₂
6 CO₂ + 6 H₂ + 3 O₂
S.w: Complete combustion of a compound containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water. Balancing: 6 C gives 6 CO₂, 12 H gives 6 H₂O, and 6 x 2 + 6 = 18 O atoms on the right match 6 + 12 = 18 on the left. The same overall equation describes cellular respiration.

n.0: This is balanced, but it leaves the oxygen unreacted; the products of complete combustion are CO₂ and H₂O.
n.2: This is balanced, but complete combustion forms CO₂, not carbon monoxide, and O₂ is consumed, not produced.
n.3: This is balanced, but hydrogen ends up as water, not H₂ gas, and oxygen gas is a reactant here, not a product.

S.q: A student is filling in a chart that compares DNA with RNA. Which features do DNA and RNA have in common? Select all that apply.
o: The sugar deoxyribose in each nucleotide
The base uracil in place of thymine
A double-stranded helical shape
Phosphate groups in the backbone
The bases guanine and cytosine
The base adenine
S.w: Both nucleic acids have a sugar-phosphate backbone and the bases A, G and C. DNA has deoxyribose and thymine and is double-stranded; RNA has ribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded.

n.0: Deoxyribose is found in DNA only; RNA contains ribose.
n.1: Uracil is found in RNA, where it replaces the thymine of DNA.
n.2: DNA is a double helix, but RNA is usually single-stranded.

S.q: Throughout a lab, a student reads the water level in each graduated cylinder while standing and looking down at the meniscus. Which statement describes the effect on the volume data?
o: The error spreads out the readings but leaves their mean accurate.
The readings become more precise because the angle is the same each time.
Readings shift the same way each time, so averaging will not remove the error.
Readings scatter in both directions, so averaging trials removes the error.
S.w: Reading from above (parallax) shifts every reading in the same direction, which is systematic error. It reduces accuracy, and averaging repeated trials cannot cancel an error that always points the same way.

n.0: Parallax from a fixed angle moves the mean away from the true value, so the mean is not accurate.
n.1: Readings can agree with one another and still be wrong; the consistent angle produces a bias, not improved quality.
n.3: This describes random error; a consistent viewing angle produces a consistent shift, not scatter.

S.q: Which set gives the correct number of separate vertebrae in each region of a typical adult's vertebral column, listed as cervical, thoracic, lumbar?
o: 5 cervical, 12 thoracic, 7 lumbar
12 cervical, 7 thoracic, 5 lumbar
7 cervical, 5 thoracic, 12 lumbar
7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar
S.w: An adult has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic (one for each pair of ribs) and 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the fused sacrum and coccyx: 26 bones in all.

n.0: This swaps the cervical and lumbar counts; the neck has 7 cervical vertebrae.
n.1: This swaps the cervical and thoracic counts; there are 12 thoracic vertebrae to match the 12 pairs of ribs.
n.2: This swaps the thoracic and lumbar counts; there are 5 large lumbar vertebrae.

S.q: The pancreas releases digestive enzymes through a duct into the small intestine and also releases insulin directly into the bloodstream. Which classification of the pancreas is correct?
o: An endocrine gland, because its enzymes act as hormones in the blood
Both an exocrine and an endocrine gland, with ducted and ductless parts
An exocrine gland, because insulin also leaves the gland through a duct
An endocrine gland, because a gland making any hormone is endocrine
S.w: Exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto a surface (the pancreatic enzymes), and endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood (insulin). The pancreas does both.

n.0: Digestive enzymes travel through a duct to the small intestine; they are exocrine secretions, not hormones.
n.2: Insulin is a hormone released directly into the blood without a duct, which is an endocrine function.
n.3: Making a hormone shows endocrine function, but the pancreas also secretes enzymes through a duct, so it is exocrine as well.

S.q: A study of 400 healthy men aged 20 to 30 finds that a daily supplement lowered their resting heart rate. Which conclusion is best supported by this study?
o: The supplement lowers resting heart rate in adults of any age.
The supplement lowers resting heart rate in women aged 60 to 70.
The supplement will lower heart rate in patients with heart disease.
The supplement lowered heart rate in the healthy young men studied.
S.w: Sound conclusions stay within the population and conditions tested. The study included only healthy men aged 20 to 30.

n.0: Adults of other ages and sexes were not tested; the result cannot be extended to them.
n.1: Older women were not studied, so this generalizes beyond the tested population.
n.2: Only healthy men took part, so the effect in heart patients is unknown.

S.q: A student rests a hand on her abdomen and feels it move outward during a normal, quiet inspiration. What is her diaphragm doing at that moment?
o: It relaxes and flattens, which lets the ribs fall and draws air in
It contracts, flattens and moves downward, enlarging the thoracic cavity
It contracts and domes upward, which pushes air into the lungs
It relaxes and domes upward, which enlarges the thoracic cavity
S.w: In inspiration the diaphragm contracts, flattens and moves down, increasing the vertical size of the thoracic cavity. The larger volume lowers pressure in the lungs, so air flows in.

n.0: A relaxed diaphragm domes upward rather than flattening, and falling ribs reduce thoracic volume.
n.2: A contracting diaphragm flattens and moves down; it does not dome upward or push air.
n.3: Relaxing and doming upward is what the diaphragm does in expiration, and it makes the thoracic cavity smaller.

S.q: Alcohol inhibits the secretion of ADH. Compared with a well-hydrated person who has not been drinking, what would be expected in a person who has had several alcoholic drinks?
o: Less water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so more dilute urine
Less water reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so less urine
More water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so less urine
More Na⁺ reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so more concentrated urine
S.w: Two steps: ADH acts on the collecting ducts to increase water reabsorption, so less ADH means less water is reabsorbed there and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced.

n.1: ADH acts on the collecting ducts, not the proximal tubule, and reabsorbing less water produces more urine, not less.
n.2: This is the effect of more ADH; alcohol lowers ADH.
n.3: Na⁺ reabsorption is controlled by aldosterone, and lower ADH makes urine more dilute, not more concentrated.

S.q: Two healthy adults have very different natural skin tones. Which difference between their skin best explains this?
o: The amount of melanin their melanocytes produce
The number of melanocytes in their stratum corneum
The number of melanocytes in their stratum basale
The amount of keratin made by their keratinocytes
S.w: People have similar numbers of melanocytes; differences in natural skin color come mainly from how much melanin those melanocytes produce (with smaller contributions from carotene and hemoglobin).

n.1: Melanocytes are located in the stratum basale, not the dead stratum corneum.
n.2: Melanocyte numbers are similar between people; it is their melanin output that differs.
n.3: Keratin is a structural, waterproofing protein, not the main pigment behind skin tone.

S.q: Which white blood cell is the most numerous in normal blood and is usually the first to arrive at a site of bacterial infection?
o: Neutrophil
Eosinophil
Monocyte
Lymphocyte
S.w: Neutrophils make up about 50-70% of white blood cells and are the first phagocytes to reach a bacterial infection; dead neutrophils form pus.

n.1: Eosinophils target parasites and take part in allergic reactions; they are a small fraction of WBCs.
n.2: Monocytes are the largest WBCs and become macrophages, but they are far fewer and arrive later.
n.3: Lymphocytes are the second most numerous (about 20-40%) and drive the specific, slower adaptive response.

S.q: Place the structures in the order light passes through them on its way to the photoreceptors, starting with the first.
o: Vitreous humor
Lens
Cornea
Aqueous humor
Pupil
Retina
S.w: Light enters through the cornea, crosses the aqueous humor, passes through the pupil (the opening in the iris), is focused by the lens, crosses the vitreous humor and reaches the photoreceptors of the retina.

S.q: After six months on a space station, an astronaut has lost bone density in the legs despite eating a normal diet. Which principle best explains this loss?
o: Bone remodels in response to the mechanical stress on it
Osteoclasts resorb bone when blood calcium rises above normal
Bone mass is fixed once the epiphyseal plates close
Calcitonin rises when the skeleton bears less weight
S.w: Bone remodeling responds to mechanical stress (Wolff's law): weight-bearing load stimulates bone formation. Without load, resorption by osteoclasts exceeds formation by osteoblasts, so bone density falls.

n.1: High blood calcium triggers calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts; resorption is driven by low blood calcium (PTH) and, in this case, by the loss of mechanical load.
n.2: Bone is remodeled throughout life; adults gain or lose bone mass long after the growth plates close.
n.3: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, so it would tend to preserve bone; it does not explain the loss.

S.q: Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen according to 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, releasing heat and light. Which classifications correctly apply to this reaction? Select all that apply.
o: Synthesis
Oxidation-reduction
Double replacement
Exothermic
Endothermic
Decomposition
S.w: Two reactants combine into one product (synthesis, A + B → AB). The reaction releases heat and light (exothermic). Hydrogen loses electrons to oxygen, so hydrogen is oxidized and oxygen is reduced (redox), as in all combustion.

n.2: Double replacement needs two compounds swapping partners; both reactants here are elements.
n.4: The reaction releases heat and light, so it is exothermic, not endothermic.
n.5: Decomposition breaks one compound apart; here two elements combine into one compound.

S.q: Besides forming urine, the kidneys perform several other functions. Which of the following are functions of the kidneys? Select all that apply.
o: Producing antidiuretic hormone
Secreting erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production
Converting ammonia into urea
Activating vitamin D to its active form, calcitriol
Secreting aldosterone into the blood
Secreting hydrogen ions and reabsorbing bicarbonate
S.w: The kidneys secrete erythropoietin, activate vitamin D (calcitriol), and help control acid-base balance by secreting H⁺ and reabsorbing or making bicarbonate. They also regulate blood volume, blood pressure and electrolytes.

n.0: ADH is made by the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary; it acts on the kidneys.
n.2: Urea is made in the liver from ammonia; the kidneys excrete it.
n.4: Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal cortex; it acts on the kidneys.

S.q: Which layer of the epidermis is the deepest and contains the dividing stem cells that replace the cells continually shed from the skin surface?
o: Stratum spinosum
Stratum corneum
Stratum basale
Stratum granulosum
S.w: The stratum basale (germinativum) is the deepest epidermal layer: a single row of dividing stem cells that push new keratinocytes upward. It also holds melanocytes and Merkel cells.

n.0: The stratum spinosum lies just above the basale and contains Langerhans cells; it is not the deepest layer.
n.1: The stratum corneum is the most superficial layer of dead, flattened, keratin-filled cells.
n.3: The stratum granulosum is a middle layer where keratinization advances and cells begin to die.

S.q: Which of these everyday phase changes releases energy to its surroundings rather than absorbing energy from them?
o: Sweat evaporating from the skin during exercise
An ice cube melting in a glass of lemonade
Water vapor condensing on a cool bathroom mirror
Mothballs subliming slowly in a closed closet
S.w: Condensation (gas to liquid) is exothermic: as vapor molecules come together and form attractions, energy is released. Freezing, condensation and deposition release heat; melting, vaporization and sublimation absorb it.

n.0: Evaporation absorbs heat from the skin, which is why sweating cools the body.
n.1: Melting is endothermic; the ice absorbs heat from the lemonade, cooling the drink.
n.3: Sublimation (solid to gas) absorbs energy, like melting and vaporization.

S.q: A heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) forms pollen grains, and each grain carries either T or t but never both. Which principle explains this?
o: The law of independent assortment
The law of dominance
Codominance of the two alleles
The law of segregation
S.w: The law of segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation (meiosis), so each gamete carries one allele.

n.0: Independent assortment concerns alleles of different genes sorting independently, not the two alleles of one gene separating.
n.1: The law of dominance explains why a Tt plant looks tall, not how its alleles are split into gametes.
n.2: Codominance is a pattern in which both alleles are expressed in the phenotype; it does not describe gamete formation.

S.q: A researcher compares the DNA of a bacterium with the DNA of a human white blood cell. Which description fits the bacterial DNA?
o: A single circular chromosome, often with plasmids
Several linear chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope
Linear chromosomes coiled around histone proteins
RNA in place of DNA, packed inside a protein capsid
S.w: Bacteria usually carry one circular chromosome in the nucleoid region, often with small extra circles of DNA called plasmids.

n.1: Multiple linear chromosomes in a nucleus describe the human (eukaryotic) cell, not the bacterium.
n.2: Histone packaging into chromatin is a eukaryotic feature.
n.3: Some viruses carry RNA inside a capsid. Bacteria are cells and store their genes in DNA.

S.q: After a car accident, a patient's ruptured spleen is surgically removed. Which normal function is most directly lost along with the spleen?
o: Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the intestine
Filtering lymph before it returns to the bloodstream
Maturing T lymphocytes before they enter circulation
Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
S.w: The spleen, the largest lymphoid organ, filters blood rather than lymph: it removes old or damaged red blood cells and platelets and mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.

n.0: Lacteals in the intestinal villi absorb dietary fats; the spleen has no part in fat absorption.
n.1: Filtering lymph is the job of the lymph nodes; the spleen filters blood.
n.2: T lymphocytes mature in the thymus, not the spleen.

S.q: After ovulation, the fimbriae sweep the secondary oocyte into the uterine tube. In a typical pregnancy, where does fertilization of the oocyte take place?
o: In the ampulla of the uterine tube
In the ruptured follicle of the ovary
In the functional layer of the endometrium
In the cervical canal of the uterus
S.w: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, the wide outer portion of the uterine tube. Cilia and peristalsis then move the developing embryo to the uterus, where it implants in the endometrium.

n.1: The oocyte leaves the ovary at ovulation; the ruptured follicle then becomes the corpus luteum.
n.2: The endometrium is where the blastocyst implants about a week later, not where fertilization occurs.
n.3: Sperm pass through the cervix on the way up; fertilization happens farther along, in the uterine tube.

S.q: Butter is solid at room temperature, while olive oil is liquid. Which difference in their fatty acids best explains this?
o: Butter's fats contain more glycerol molecules per fatty acid.
Olive oil's fatty acids carry more hydrogen atoms per carbon.
Butter's fatty acids are mostly saturated and pack tightly together.
Butter's fatty acids have more C=C double bonds, which form kinks.
S.w: Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, so their straight chains pack tightly and the fat is solid. Unsaturated fatty acids in oils have double bonds that kink the chains.

n.0: Every triglyceride has one glycerol and three fatty acids; the difference is saturation.
n.1: This is reversed: saturated fatty acids such as butter's carry the most hydrogen. Olive oil's C=C double bonds mean fewer hydrogens.
n.3: This is reversed: double bonds and kinks belong to unsaturated fats, which are liquid.

S.q: When the stomach is empty, its inner lining forms large folds that flatten out as a meal arrives. What are these folds called, and what is their main role?
o: Rugae, which allow the stomach to expand with food
Microvilli, which hold brush-border digestive enzymes
Circular folds, which slow chyme to aid absorption
Villi, which add surface area for absorbing nutrients
S.w: Rugae are the folds of the stomach lining. They flatten as the stomach fills, letting it stretch to hold a meal.

n.1: Microvilli form the brush border of small intestine cells, not folds of the stomach lining.
n.2: Circular folds belong to the small intestine wall and do not flatten when the stomach fills.
n.3: Villi are finger-like projections of the small intestine, not stomach folds.

S.q: Which statements about the hormonal control of the testes are correct? Select all that apply.
o: FSH and testosterone together stimulate spermatogenesis via Sertoli cells.
FSH from the posterior pituitary acts on the Sertoli cells.
Testosterone raises GnRH output by positive feedback on the hypothalamus.
LH stimulates interstitial (Leydig) cells to secrete testosterone.
Leydig cells line the seminiferous tubules and nourish developing sperm.
Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH release.
S.w: LH acts on Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone. FSH, together with testosterone, acts through the Sertoli cells to drive spermatogenesis. Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH.

n.1: FSH is released by the anterior pituitary, not the posterior pituitary.
n.2: Testosterone exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH and LH.
n.4: Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells, line the tubules and nourish developing sperm; Leydig cells sit between the tubules.

E.q: Read the sentence: "The nurse who works nights trained the student whom we hired." How many dependent clauses does it contain?
o: Three
Zero
Two
One
E.w: There are two relative clauses, each with its own subject and verb: "who works nights" and "whom we hired". The independent clause is "The nurse trained the student".

n.0: "The nurse trained the student" is the independent clause, so it is not counted.
n.1: Clauses beginning with relative pronouns (who, whom) are dependent clauses.
n.3: Both "who works nights" and "whom we hired" are dependent clauses, not just one.

E.q: A tutor gives a student six sentences from a patient handout. Which sentences are simple sentences? Select all that apply.
o: The staff stayed calm because the night was quiet.
If the form is signed, the nurse will file it.
The aide lifted the patient, and the nurse adjusted the bed.
The aide lifted the patient carefully and adjusted the bed.
Both the doctor and the nurse signed the form.
During the long night shift, the staff stayed calm.
E.w: Each simple sentence has one independent clause: a compound subject, an introductory prepositional phrase or a compound verb does not add a clause.

n.0: "Because the night was quiet" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.1: "If the form is signed" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by ", and" make a compound sentence.

E.q: Luis is writing an argumentative essay about school start times. Which sentence would work best as his thesis statement?
o: In this essay, I will discuss the start times of high schools across the country.
Many high schools in the United States begin classes before 8:30 in the morning.
High schools should start after 8:30 a.m. to improve teens' sleep and grades.
Should high schools start later in the morning so that teenagers get more sleep?
E.w: An effective thesis makes one specific, arguable claim and can preview the main points. This sentence takes a clear position (start after 8:30 a.m.) and names the reasons the essay will develop (sleep and grades).

n.0: This is an announcement of the topic ("In this essay, I will"); it states no position for the essay to argue.
n.1: This is a statement of fact that no one would dispute, so there is nothing to argue.
n.3: A question is not a thesis; the thesis should answer the question with a claim.

E.q: A school nurse is writing a newsletter paragraph about dehydration. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: When the body loses more fluid than it takes in, blood volume drops.
Dehydration can develop quickly during a summer heat wave.
For this reason, health officials urge people to drink water before they feel thirsty.
Over time, a person may feel dizzy, tired or confused.
As a result, the heart must work harder to supply the organs.
E.w: The topic sentence comes first, then a chain of causes and effects: fluid loss lowers blood volume, "As a result" the heart works harder, "Over time" symptoms appear, and "For this reason" gives the advice that follows.

E.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "By the time the team was ____ to begin, the patient had ____ been discharged."
o: all ready; already
all ready; all ready
already; all ready
already; already
E.w: "All ready" means completely prepared (the team was all ready to begin); "already" means by this time (had already been discharged).

n.1: "Had all ready been discharged" needs the time word "already".
n.2: Both are reversed: being prepared is "all ready", and "by this time" is "already".
n.3: Being completely prepared is "all ready"; "was already to begin" does not make sense.

E.q: Read the paragraph from a student's research summary. (1) A recent study examined how evening screen time affects sleep in adolescents. (2) Teens who used their phones after 9 p.m. got a lot less sleep. (3) On average, they slept 48 minutes less than peers who did not use phones at night. (4) These findings suggest that limiting evening screen use may improve rest. Which sentence does not match the formal register of the paragraph?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
E.w: Sentence 2 uses informal wording ("teens," "got," "a lot less"). A formal version: "Adolescents who used their phones after 9 p.m. slept less."

n.0: Sentence 1 is formal: precise terms ("adolescents," "evening screen time") and an objective tone.
n.1: Sentence 3 is formal: it reports a specific figure in standard language.
n.2: Sentence 4 is formal: "suggest" and "may" state the conclusion with appropriate caution.

E.q: Read the paragraph from a scholarship essay. (1) Last spring, Keisha volunteered at a free clinic in her town. (2) She checks in patients and took their blood pressure. (3) The experience showed her how much she enjoyed patient care. (4) By June, she had decided to apply to nursing school. Which sentence contains an unnecessary shift in verb tense?
o: Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
E.w: Sentence 2 shifts from present ("checks") to past ("took") while describing the same past events; it should read "She checked in patients and took..."

n.0: "Had decided" is past perfect, correctly marking a decision completed by a past point ("By June").
n.1: "Showed" and "enjoyed" are both simple past, consistent with the rest of the paragraph.
n.2: "Volunteered" is simple past, which matches "last spring."

E.q: Kiara is writing a research paper on teen vaping for her health class. Which of her activities belong to the prewriting stage? Select all that apply.
o: Formatting the final copy for submission
Building an outline of main points and support
Rewriting her conclusion so it restates the thesis
Narrowing her broad topic to a manageable focus
Correcting comma splices in her second paragraph
Gathering research on the topic before writing
E.w: Prewriting is planning: identifying purpose and audience, choosing and narrowing the topic, generating ideas, researching and outlining. Narrowing the topic, researching and outlining all happen before any drafting.

n.0: Preparing and submitting the final copy is publishing, the last stage.
n.2: Rewriting a conclusion to restate the thesis improves the content of an existing draft, which is revising.
n.4: Fixing comma splices is a sentence-level correction, which is editing.

E.q: A travel nurse lists the cities on her contract schedule. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The tour stops in Boise; Idaho, Reno; Nevada, and Provo; Utah.
The tour stops in: Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
The tour stops in Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
The tour stops in Boise, Idaho, Reno, Nevada, and Provo, Utah.
E.w: When series items already contain commas (city, state), semicolons separate the items so each pair stays together.

n.0: The semicolons are placed inside each pair instead of between the pairs.
n.1: A colon must not follow a preposition such as "in".
n.3: With commas only, the reader cannot tell where one city-state pair ends and the next begins.

E.q: An infection-control poster uses sentences with different purposes. Which sentence is imperative?
o: You washed your hands before you entered the patient's room.
Did you wash your hands before you entered the patient's room?
Please wash your hands before you enter the patient's room.
What a relief it was to wash my hands after that long shift!
E.w: An imperative sentence gives a command or makes a request, with the subject "you" understood: "[You] Please wash your hands."

n.0: This makes a statement, so it is declarative.
n.1: This asks a question, so it is interrogative.
n.3: This expresses strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

E.q: A student is writing a formal research paper on sleep and academic performance. Which sentence is most appropriate for this paper?
o: Students who sleep fewer than six hours tend to earn lower grades.
Research shows that students who skimp on sleep see their grades tank.
Students who don't get enough sleep tend to earn lower grades.
You'd be surprised how much your sleep affects your final grades.
E.w: Formal academic writing uses third person, precise wording, no contractions and no slang, and states claims objectively.

n.1: Slang ("skimp on," "tank") does not suit academic writing, even when a source is mentioned.
n.2: The contraction "don't" and the vague "enough" are informal and imprecise for a formal research paper.
n.3: Second person ("you") and a contraction ("You'd") are too conversational for a formal paper.

E.q: A physical therapy assistant is writing notes after a session. Which sentence uses "rise" or "raise" correctly?
o: Prices for the required nursing textbooks have raised every semester.
The therapist asked the patient to rise his arm above his head.
The patient's temperature rose overnight, so we called the doctor.
The aide raised from her chair when the surgeon entered the room.
E.w: "Rise" (rise, rose, risen) has no object; "raise" (raise, raised, raised) takes one. A temperature goes up by itself, so "rose" is correct.

n.0: Prices go up on their own (no object), so the verb must be "risen": "have risen."
n.1: Lifting an arm takes an object ("his arm"), so the verb must be "raise."
n.3: Getting up has no object, so the verb must be "rose" (past of "rise").

E.q: A unit has twelve patients, and only one of them fell yesterday. Which sentence correctly identifies that particular patient?
o: The patient who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
E.w: Two steps: with twelve patients, "who fell yesterday" is essential (restrictive) because it identifies which patient. Essential clauses take no commas.

n.1: A comma must not separate the subject from its verb (needs).
n.2: A single comma after "patient" opens an aside that is never closed.
n.3: Commas would mark the clause as nonessential, as if there were only one patient; here it is needed to identify the patient.

E.q: A nursing instructor asks students to identify a compound-complex sentence in a set of examples. Which sentence is compound-complex?
o: Ana and Ben missed the bus and arrived late to the lecture.
Because Ana missed the bus, she arrived late to the lecture.
Ana arrived on time, but Ben, who missed the bus, was late.
Ana missed the bus, so she arrived late to the lecture.
E.w: Two independent clauses (Ana arrived on time; Ben was late) plus a dependent relative clause (who missed the bus) make a compound-complex sentence.

n.0: One independent clause with a compound subject and compound verb is a simple sentence.
n.1: One dependent clause and one independent clause make a complex sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses with no dependent clause make a compound sentence.

E.q: A wellness coordinator is writing a poster about rest. Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
o: One factor: mattered most to the team, getting enough sleep.
One factor mattered most to the team: getting enough sleep.
One factor mattered most to the team; getting enough sleep.
The factor that mattered most was: getting enough sleep.
E.w: A colon after a complete independent clause can introduce an explanation or example: "getting enough sleep" explains the factor.

n.0: A colon must not separate a subject (One factor) from its verb (mattered).
n.2: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; "getting enough sleep" is a phrase.
n.3: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "was".

E.q: A nursing student is editing a shift report that joins two complete thoughts with a coordinating conjunction. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The nurse checked the patient's chart, and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart, and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse, checked the patient's chart and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
E.w: When a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before the conjunction: "chart, and the doctor".

n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "and" is needed.
n.2: The comma belongs before the conjunction, not after it.
n.3: A comma must not separate a subject (The nurse) from its verb (checked), and the comma before "and" is missing.

E.q: A nursing club is printing a flyer about clinical placements. Which sentence on the flyer uses the pronouns "we" and "us" correctly?
o: Us students were asked to arrive by 6:30 a.m. for clinicals.
The new policy was explained to we volunteers on Monday.
The instructor gave us students extra time on the dosage exam.
Several of we applicants had questions about the essay prompt.
E.w: Drop the noun to test: "The instructor gave us extra time" is correct, so "gave us students" is correct. "Us" is the indirect object of "gave."

n.0: Drop "students": "Us were asked" is wrong. The phrase is the subject, so it must be "We students."
n.1: Drop "volunteers": "explained to we" is wrong. The object of "to" needs "us volunteers."
n.3: "Of" is a preposition, so its object needs the objective case: "several of us applicants."

E.q: A nursing student is emailing her pharmacology professor to ask for a meeting about a failed exam. Which sentence is most appropriate for this audience and purpose?
o: I hereby request an audience at your earliest convenience regarding my examination.
I will stop by your office at noon tomorrow to go over my exam.
I would like to schedule a meeting to discuss my recent exam results.
I was hoping we might talk soon about a few things from class.
E.w: An email to a professor calls for formal, polite language that states the purpose clearly: a meeting about exam results.

n.0: "I hereby request an audience" is inflated, stiff wording; a clear, polite request suits an email to a professor.
n.1: The writer announces a visit instead of asking for one, which is presumptuous toward the professor.
n.3: The request is vague ("a few things from class"); it never says the meeting is about the exam.

E.q: As part of a rehabilitation assessment after a stroke, the occupational therapist tested the patient's manual dexterity. Based on its root, which body part does manual dexterity involve?
o: The feet
The voice
The hands
The eyes
E.w: The root man/manu means hand, so manual dexterity is skill in using the hands.

n.0: Foot is the meaning of ped/pod (as in podiatrist).
n.1: Voice is the meaning of voc/vok (as in vocal).
n.3: Eye or sight comes from vis/vid or ocul/o, not manu.

E.q: A mother brings her toddler to the clinic with a mild cold, a low fever, and persistent rhinorrhea. Based on its word parts, what is rhinorrhea?
o: Inflammation of the nose
A discharge from the nose
Bleeding from the nose
Surgical repair of the nose
E.w: rhin/o means nose and -rrhea means flow or discharge, so rhinorrhea is a runny nose.

n.0: Inflammation of the nose is rhinitis (-itis).
n.2: Bleeding (bursting forth) is -rrhage or -rrhagia, the look-alike suffix.
n.3: Surgical repair is -plasty (rhinoplasty).

E.q: Jordan is drafting the thesis for an argumentative essay on hospital visiting hours. Which qualities would make his thesis statement effective? Select all that apply.
o: It makes a specific claim that a reader could dispute
It is narrow enough to support in the essay's length
It previews the main points the essay will develop
It states a fact that most readers already accept
It poses a question for the essay to explore
It opens with "In this essay, I will discuss"
E.w: An effective thesis is one sentence that states a specific, focused, arguable claim and often previews the main points. It must also be narrow enough to develop fully in the space available.

n.3: A widely accepted fact gives the essay nothing to argue.
n.4: A question is not a thesis; the thesis answers the question with a position.
n.5: An announcement names the topic but takes no position, so it is not a thesis.

E.q: A wellness flyer reads: "Regular exercise strengthens the heart and lungs. ___, it can improve the quality of a person's sleep." Which transition best completes the flyer?
o: In other words
Conversely
Specifically
In addition
E.w: The second sentence adds another benefit of exercise. "In addition" signals addition.

n.0: "In other words" restates the same idea, but better sleep is a new point, not a restatement.
n.1: "Conversely" signals an opposite idea, but better sleep is another benefit, not an opposite.
n.2: "Specifically" narrows the previous idea, but sleep quality is not a detail of heart and lung strength.

E.q: A student is editing a reflection paper about a clinical skills lab. Which sentence from the paper uses pronoun case correctly?
o: Him and his sister both applied to the nursing program this year.
Between you and me, the new skills schedule is an improvement.
The instructor asked Maria and I to demonstrate the bed transfer.
The award went to Devon and myself for the hand-hygiene project.
E.w: "Between" is a preposition, and the object of a preposition takes the objective case: "between you and me."

n.0: "Him and his sister" is the subject, so the subjective case is needed: "He and his sister."
n.2: "Maria and I" is the object of "asked," so the objective case is needed: "asked Maria and me." Drop "Maria and" to test: "asked me."
n.3: "Myself" is reflexive and has no antecedent in the sentence; the object of "to" needs "me": "to Devon and me."

E.q: A student is classifying sentences from a hospital orientation booklet by structure. Which of the following is a compound sentence?
o: The nurse and the aide checked and recorded the vital signs.
The clinic opened early, but the lab stayed closed until nine.
Because the lab was closed, the samples waited until morning.
When the storm hit, the power failed, and the generator started.
E.w: A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses and no dependent clause. "The clinic opened early" and "the lab stayed closed until nine" are joined by a comma and "but".

n.0: This is a simple sentence: one independent clause with a compound subject (nurse and aide) and a compound verb (checked and recorded).
n.2: This is complex: "Because the lab was closed" is a dependent clause attached to one independent clause.
n.3: This is compound-complex: two independent clauses plus the dependent clause "When the storm hit".

E.q: A nurse is documenting how long a procedure took. Which sentence uses "than" and "then" correctly?
o: The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
E.w: "Than" makes a comparison (longer than expected); "then" shows time or sequence (and then left).

n.0: "And ___ left" shows sequence, so it needs "then".
n.1: Both are reversed: the comparison needs "than" and the sequence needs "then".
n.2: "Longer ___ expected" is a comparison, so it needs "than".

E.q: Original sentence: "Frequent handwashing is the single most effective way to stop the spread of infection in hospitals." Which version, with a citation added, is an acceptable paraphrase?
o: Frequent handwashing is the most effective way to stop infection from spreading in hospitals.
In hospitals, the best way to keep infections from spreading is for staff to wash their hands often.
Frequent hand cleaning is the single most useful way to halt the spread of infection in hospitals.
Hospitals should place handwashing stations in every patient room to cut infection rates.
E.w: An acceptable paraphrase keeps the original meaning but uses the writer's own words and sentence structure. This version reorders the sentence (starting with the setting) and rewords it while keeping the same idea.

n.0: This keeps almost all of the original wording and structure, which is patchwriting, a form of plagiarism even with a citation.
n.2: Swapping a few synonyms into the original sentence structure is still patchwriting.
n.3: This adds a new recommendation the original never made, so it does not restate the source's idea.

E.q: The hospital's quality committee reviewed mortality data from the past year to compare outcomes across its units. Based on its root, what do mortality data measure?
o: The number of diseases diagnosed
The number of deaths
The number of patients transferred
The number of births
E.w: The root mort means death, so mortality data measure deaths (for example, deaths per 1,000 patients).

n.0: Disease is the meaning of path (as in pathology).
n.2: Transfer relates to port (carry) or mit (send), not mort.
n.3: Births relate to natal (as in prenatal), not mort.

E.q: A warning label on a can of cleaning solvent reads, "Inflammable: store away from heat, sparks, and open flames." Based on the context, what does inflammable mean?
o: Safe to store near heat
Unable to catch fire
Harmful if breathed in
Easily set on fire
E.w: Here in- does not mean not: inflammable means the same as flammable. The context (keep it away from heat, sparks and flames) confirms that the product catches fire easily.

n.0: This also reads in- as "not," which contradicts the instruction to store it away from heat.
n.1: This reads in- as "not," but the warning to keep the can away from flames shows it can catch fire.
n.2: The label's warning is about fire, and nothing in the word parts refers to breathing.

E.q: Jada has one sister-in-law, who owns a car. Which sentence correctly shows that the car belongs to that one sister-in-law?
o: My sisters-in-law's car is in the shop.
My sister's-in-law car is in the shop.
My sister-in-law's car is in the shop.
My sister-in-laws car is in the shop.
E.w: A compound noun forms its possessive on the last word: "sister-in-law's". The singular form is used because there is one owner.

n.0: "Sisters-in-law's" is the plural possessive, but Jada has only one sister-in-law.
n.1: The possessive ending goes on the last word of the compound, not the first.
n.3: "Sister-in-laws" has no apostrophe, so it is not a possessive.

E.q: A nurse is writing a reflective journal entry. Which sentence punctuates the adjectives correctly?
o: It was a long, tiring shift in the busy, emergency room.
It was a long, tiring, shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
E.w: "Long" and "tiring" are coordinate adjectives (they could be joined by "and"), so a comma separates them. "Emergency room" is a compound noun, so "busy" takes no comma.

n.0: "Emergency" is part of the noun "emergency room", so no comma follows "busy".
n.1: No comma goes between the last adjective and the noun it modifies.
n.2: Coordinate adjectives that each describe the noun separately are separated by a comma: "long, tiring".

E.q: A medical terminology instructor asks students to work out the meaning of in- from context. In which sentence does the prefix in- mean "not"?
o: The tumor was found to be inoperable.
The nurse will inject the vaccine into the upper arm.
Patients should inhale slowly through the mouth.
Insert the catheter gently into the opening.
E.w: in- can mean not or into. In inoperable it means not: the tumor is not able to be operated on.

n.1: In inject, in- means into: to throw (ject) medicine into the body.
n.2: In inhale, in- means into: to breathe in.
n.3: In insert, in- means into: to put something into an opening.

E.q: A school nurse is making a sign to hang above the sink in a second-grade classroom. Which sentence is most appropriate for these readers?
o: Wash your hands with soap before you eat.
Wash your hands with soap prior to consuming food.
Perform hand hygiene before you eat.
Hand washing reduces the spread of germs.
E.w: Young readers need short sentences, simple everyday words and a clear action to take.

n.1: "Prior to consuming food" is formal wording that young children may not know.
n.2: "Perform hand hygiene" is health-care jargon that seven-year-old readers may not understand.
n.3: This states a general fact but does not tell the children what to do at the sink.

E.q: Read the paragraph from a county health report. (1) In 2015, the county had one free clinic. (2) By 2020, it had three, plus a mobile health van. (3) Last year, two more clinics opened in rural towns. (4) Access to free health care in the county has grown steadily over the past decade. Which sentence is the topic sentence?
o: Sentence 2
Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 3
E.w: This paragraph moves from specific to general: the details come first, and sentence 4 states the main idea they support.

n.0: Sentence 2 is another specific detail about the number of clinics in 2020.
n.1: Sentence 1 is a specific detail (one clinic in 2015); being first does not make it the main idea.
n.3: Sentence 3 is a specific detail about last year's openings.

E.q: A US health department is editing a brochure for American readers. Which sentence follows standard American spelling throughout?
o: The center will analyze each patient's behaviour.
The center will analyze each patient's behavior.
The center will analyse each patient's behavior.
The centre will analyze each patient's behavior.
E.w: American English uses -er (center), -yze (analyze) and -or (behavior). Each other version slips in one British spelling.

n.0: "Behaviour" is the British spelling; American English drops the u: "behavior".
n.2: "Analyse" is the British spelling; American English uses "analyze".
n.3: "Centre" is the British spelling; American English uses "center".

E.q: An instructor is grading sentences on a grammar quiz for first-year nursing students. Which sentences use pronouns correctly? Select all that apply.
o: Whom should the front desk call if the results are late?
The tutor helped Grace and myself with dosage problems.
The award was shared by Mei and her.
Dev and me will cover the weekend shifts in March.
Each of the clinics posted its holiday hours online.
E.w: "Each" is singular, so "its" agrees. "By Mei and her" uses the objective case after the preposition "by." "Whom" is the object of "call" (the desk should call him).

n.1: "Myself" has no antecedent in the sentence; the object of "helped" needs "me": "Grace and me."
n.3: "Dev and me" is the subject, so it needs the subjective case: "Dev and I will cover."

E.q: Lucia wants to use one sentence, word for word, from a nursing journal in her APA-style paper. Which combination of elements must she include?
o: Quotation marks plus a reference-list entry, with no in-text citation
Quotation marks plus an in-text citation and a reference-list entry
Quotation marks plus an in-text citation, with no reference-list entry
An in-text citation and a reference-list entry, without quotation marks
E.w: Exact words need quotation marks to show they are copied. APA then requires both an in-text citation in the body and a full entry in the reference list at the end of the paper.

n.0: Without an in-text citation, the reader cannot tell which source the quotation comes from at the point it is used.
n.2: Every source cited in the text must also appear in the reference list.
n.3: Copied words without quotation marks are presented as her own wording, which is plagiarism even with citations.

E.q: During a dressing change, the nurse documented a malodorous discharge from the patient's wound and notified the provider. Based on its prefix, what does malodorous mean?
o: Having no smell
Having a faint smell
Having a bad smell
Having a pleasant smell
E.w: mal- means bad, and odor means smell, so malodorous means having a bad smell.

n.0: No smell would use a- or an- (without), not mal-.
n.1: Faint (less than normal) would match hypo-, not mal-.
n.3: A pleasant smell is the opposite of mal- (bad); good would be eu- or bene.
